Today, the recipe used to optimize a deep neural network is typically completely determined before training even begins. A great deal of human ingenuity has gone into priors regarding how training should progress: adaptive step sizes [1], preconditioning [2, 3], orthogonalized updates [4, 5], schedules tied to the training step [6, 7], and learning rates scaled with model size [8]. Automated discovery [9, 10, 11, 12] searches across many runs for better optimizers. Whether hand-crafted or automatically discovered, the optimizer then runs unchanged through the end of training, adapting, if at all, according to rules written in advance. This scope leaves the following questions unanswered: How should an optimizer respond to an unexpected loss spike or stall? What if one module’s gradients start to oscillate while the others keep improving smoothly? And when a new type of architecture trains poorly with Adam or Muon, is the architecture worse, or has it not yet met an optimizer suited to it?
In this post, we attempt to expand the scope of conventional optimizers and make them reactive to the training itself, leading to an ever-adapting optimizer inside a single training run. This reactive optimizer reasons on the spot and writes the weight update rule for each parameter group. Directly writing optimization code, it has the freedom to implement complicated schedules, respond to training accidents, and customize the optimizer for the single training episode in which it exists. Building on earlier attempts to adapt optimizers during training [12, 13, 14] and to let a model direct its own fine-tuning [15], the reactive optimizer is entirely zero-shot, with nothing learned or retained from repeated runs, and puts the optimizer’s entire algorithm up for rewriting.
We start with a practical situation, with tasks from image generation and language modeling, in which a reactive optimizer can do much better than static ones. We then turn to the emergent properties of the reactive optimizer, including sophisticated scheduling, suppressing loss spikes, and escaping overfitting. Lastly, we ask what all this costs and how practical it is at scale. We expect the reactive optimizer to grow only stronger with each generation of agents, to be most useful exactly where no recipe exists yet (for a new architecture or a new dataset), and to be one step toward solving the puzzles of deep learning optimization.
Contents
1. Training without a recipe
2. Updating with spontaneous analysis
3. What is dynamically changing during optimization?
4. Real-world applicability
5. Conclusion
1. Training without a recipe
Suppose a PhD student has a new idea: a model of their own design, or a new dataset on which to train a transformer. They have one GPU for a single day only and a modest allotment of LLM API tokens, allowing for just one serious training run. What should the student do? The obvious course of action would be to pick the most standard training recipe, or one from a recent paper, and cope with the possibility that it might be unsuitable for their scenario, with spiking/stalling loss, etc.
The underlying question is broader: when bounded by GPU time, researcher time, or wall-clock time, how can a deep learning model be trained to its best performance without knowing the optimal optimization recipe in advance? New architectures, modalities, languages, and scientific data all fall into this setting, where few people can afford a sweep at scale.
A reactive optimizer offers another way to use that budget: it spends LLM tokens in place of GPU/human hours. With optimizers reacting to training incidents and adjusting themselves, much of the burden of recipe tuning can be reduced.
Results in brief
We start from the optimization track (Track 3) of modded-nanogpt [16], a language-model pre-training task (training a 162M GPT on FineWeb) with many recipes tuned specifically for this one setting. From this task, we create two slightly differing natural settings: (1) the same model trained on an alternate language dataset (we select Chinese, Thai, and Kyrgyz), and (2) the original setup with a quarter of the batch size. Neither comes with a recipe tuned for that setting, so we compare the reactive optimizer with the natural options one would have if they wanted to one-shot the new training: adopting five leaderboard recipes with natural adjustments. In all these new settings, the reactive optimizer outperforms or matches the best baseline (Figure 1).
We also apply the reactive optimizer directly to Goldfish [17], which proposes a dataset of 350 languages and trains one small GPT per dataset with a standard recipe not tuned for each language. This makes it an ideal ground to test the optimizer’s adaptiveness in one shot. On the Amharic dataset, the official recipe ends at 83.48 bits per sentence on held-out FLORES-200 text (lower is better); the reactive optimizer, initialized with this same recipe, ends at 81.11 in one shot (on Swahili, we obtain a similar gain). Sweeping the learning rate of the standard recipe finds a static recipe that ends ahead of the reactive optimizer, at 80.89, but the reactive optimizer initialized from that swept recipe ends ahead again, at 80.73.
We also try the reactive optimizer on image generation, a direction where the literature usually does not sweep optimization hyperparameters, since diffusion-model design and optimizer design are viewed as mostly orthogonal1
1 For example, the standard recipes of DiT and SiT [19] train with AdamW at one constant learning rate. That has begun to change, with Muon and its variants taken up for diffusion transformers (CMuon [20]; Li et al. [21]; RAEv2’s GMuon [22]) and a recent controlled benchmark of optimizers for diffusion models [23].
. It ends ahead of the official recipe on LightningDiT-XL/1 ([18]; FID-50K 1.83 against 2.18 with guidance, 4.33 against 5.15 without), whose official recipe trains with AdamW, and on RAEv2-B (3.19 against 3.39), whose recipe trains with a Muon variant.
Figure 1 shows these runs, each with Claude Opus 5.5 powering the agent; we name our reactive optimizer OPAL (OPtimizer with an Agent in the Loop). Together, these results show that in one-shot settings, a reactive optimizer can lead to a better solution than adhering to a predetermined recipe.

Beyond the practical benefit, we are intrigued by the spontaneous decisions made by the zero-shot agent, after observing and analyzing the training dynamics in its own way. In the next two sections, we explore what the reactive optimizer chooses to watch and what it changes in response.
2. Updating with spontaneous analysis

Figure 2. The two programs the agent writes and rewrites iteratively during training. With code as the entire interface, we give the agent maximal freedom to choose what to watch and what to change.
Figure 2 shows how an agent updates the optimizer code on the fly. Concretely, we allow the agent to rewrite a file, updater.py, used in every step of optimization. We use code as the entire interface since this allows the agent to easily alter any part of the optimization. Yet, before the agent can make changes, it must observe, on its own, how training is progressing, leading to the second program it can rewrite, analysis.py.
What information should the agent use to make its decisions? Raw training states would be impractical: the weights, activations, and gradients would swamp its context. Instead, the statistics and geometry of training dynamics could be helpful for decisions, such as the gradient norm of each parameter group, the size of an update next to the weights it changes, the cosine between consecutive gradients, and which tensors exhibit unusually large gradient spikes. Therefore, as with the optimizer, we give the agent the most freedom: it writes a program, analysis.py, to extract whatever it wants to know from the training dynamics. Its self-written probes run throughout training, taking from the state of training whatever the agent asks for and handing it to the agent for its next decision.
We complete the bidirectional loop. Through analysis.py, training reaches the agent in whatever form the agent chooses to see it, and through updater.py, the agent’s decisions reach every step of training. The two programs let the agent devise new optimization algorithms along the way with maximum flexibility.
3. What is dynamically changing during optimization?
In this section, we look at what the reactive optimizer does throughout training, examining the decisions behind these results. As a summary, Figure 3 shows when, how, and why each agent edits its code.

Frontier training runs come with elaborate hyperparameter schedules, such as the five stages of DeepSeek-V3’s learning rate ([24]; Figure 4, left), with such schedules sometimes being written by humans during the training process [25]. Engineers can make only so many decisions, each weighing only so many signals. A reactive optimizer can take over this work and has no such limit: it decides frequently, and at each decision, it can access the entire history of the run. As Figure 4 shows, the schedules our agents built are intricate, with separate multi-stage schedules for each parameter group, and differ from run to run. Several of them raise a learning rate mid-run, a move rarely seen in modern schedulers, yet naturally helpful in many scenarios [6, 26]. Moreover, the four examples below show the evidence they cited for their decisions.
We observe that the agents base these decisions on the diagnostics from analysis.py. Some examples are: the cosine between a module’s consecutive gradients as a sign of overshooting (see “Deduced from clues” below); A/B testing between two learning rates every few hundred updates, comparing how fast the loss falls under each (“A-B-A test”); trial and error, with the learning rate raised, lowered, and raised again (“Trial and error”); and the trend of the loss, which makes agents start their cooldown earlier than planned (“Re-planned cooldown”). Each of these changes of schedule involves observation of the training dynamics and reasoning upon said observations.

Code: bbtree, scc TreeIndex, concurrent-map, crossbeam SkipMap.
On this page
What can it do?
Case 1: faster memtable
Case 2: database index
Case 3: bbtree-mmap
How it works?
1Minimize cache misses
2Minimize instructions
3Minimize cache coherence traffic
How do we make it correct?
Guard 1: Xiangpeng Hao
Guard 2: LLMs
Guard 3: fuzzing, verification, DSTs
Reviewers of this post
What can it do?
B-trees are the most important data structure in big data systems, a fast b-tree like bbtree benefits everything on top of it: agents memory, LLM training, RAG, KV store, state caching, vector search, and more.
Here we discuss three representative use cases:
Replace skiplist in LSM-trees. In place of the skiplist of four LSM-trees, bbtree is 1.37–6.83× faster.
In-memory database index. In place of Turso's skiplists, inserts are 2.22× and indexed SELECTs 1.90× faster.
Mmap a bbtree from disk. No rebuild after a restart: the first answer comes 160–2,500× sooner than std's BTreeMap.
Case 1: faster memtable
Case 2: database index
Case 3: bbtree-mmap
All LSM-trees use an ordered map to hold recent writes in memory, the memtable. In Rust, this ordered map is usually a skiplist, like crossbeam-skiplist.
bbtree can easily replace it and is much faster. A skiplist takes a cache miss for almost every node it visits on its way down; a bbtree lookup touches a handful of cache lines (see How it works, below).
bbtree has a similar interface as crossbeam-skiplist but simpler: there is no epoch, no need to worry about when to pin or re-enter an epoch.
bbtree allows more advanced memory management:
Custom allocator is supported on day one.
It never allocates on irregular sizes (i.e., not a power of two): memory management stays easy, with no external fragmentation2
2Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, Free-Space Management, chapter 17 of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: external fragmentation is free space chopped into pieces of different sizes, so that a request can fail although the total would fit it.
.
Allocation failure can be gracefully handled.
We integrated bbtree into four LSM-trees, on each system's own benchmarks:
fjall: gets 2.47×, inserts 1.61×, write batches 3.00×.
SlateDB: gets 1.71×, puts 1.65×, write batches of 10 rows 2.36×.
Tonbo: 10M-row writes 6.83×, conflict-checked transactions 4.10×.
Lance's MemWAL index (its own skiplist): point lookups 2.19×, batched lookups 3.94×, batched puts 4.21×.
The LSM-trees of the End to End card: each system's own benchmark, one thread, Ryzen 9 9900X. The dark bar is the time per operation as shipped, the bright one inside it with bbtree; only the map changed.
Next, 2 of 3
Case 2: database index
→
How it works?
Every performance optimization should be guided by a cost model.
B-tree optimizations are simple, three easy pieces3
3Not more complicated than an operating system! Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (2016).
: we just need to remember three principles, in order:
The number of chained cache lines touched. A cache miss costs about 100 ns.
The number of instructions executed. An instruction costs about 0.5 ns.
The amount of cache coherence traffic, especially important for concurrent access. It forces a cache miss, and costs a little more than 100 ns.
1
Minimize cache misses
2
Minimize instructions
3
Minimize cache coherence traffic
With this cost model, it's clear that the most important optimization is to minimize the number of cache misses. To put it another way, for each cache miss, we want to narrow down the search space as much as we can.
Thought experiment: binary search vs linear search
Say we have a sorted array of u64s, and we want to find a target u64.
With binary search, each cache miss narrows down the search space by half.
With linear search, each cache miss narrows down the search space by cache_line_size / item_size items, which is 64 / 8 = 8.
So the break-even point is about 16 items, where binary search costs the same as linear search: two cache misses to find the target.
But there's a catch: 1. the CPU prefetcher may fetch the next cache lines on its own, which gives linear search an even bigger advantage; 2. linear search is simpler, allowing much more parallelism in the CPU pipeline. So the actual break-even point is usually higher.
64 sorted u64s, 8 to a cache line. Each step is one cache miss: binary search halves what is left, linear search rules out one line. Here binary search needs 3 misses and linear search 6; at 16 items, both need at most 2.
Pause
How does that apply to B-trees?
In a B-tree, this decides the node size4
4Jun Rao and Kenneth A. Ross, Making B+-Trees Cache Conscious in Main Memory (SIGMOD 2000).
. If we size nodes so that each holds about 16–32 items, we can always do linear search, which lets us do nice things like SIMD (in later sections).
What if the keys are Strings? Strings are different, because their bytes are stored on the heap, not inline in the node. This changes our equation completely. We no longer get 8 keys from one cache miss; instead, each key we load is its own cache miss. So we almost always want to do binary search over Strings.
A node of Strings holds each key's pointer, length and capacity; its bytes are on the heap. Every comparison of a binary search follows a pointer: 3 heap reads to find one key of 8.
Pause
How does bbtree do it? Heap keys are very common, so bbtree must handle them well. bbtree introduces inline_keys, an idea databases have used for decades5,6
5Goetz Graefe and Per-Åke Larson, B-Tree Indexes and CPU Caches (ICDE 2001).
6Goetz Graefe, More Modern B-Tree Techniques (2024): keep full keys out of the comparison stream with dense, fixed-width codes, and skip the prefix a page shares.
, similar to German strings7
7Thomas Neumann and Michael Freitag, Umbra: A Disk-Based System with In-Memory Performance (CIDR 2020); see also my post on the nature of strings.
and StringView in Arrow8
8Xiangpeng Hao and Andrew Lamb, Using StringView / German Style Strings to Make Queries Faster: Part 1, Reading Parquet and Part 2, String Operations (2024).
.
With fixed-size inline keys, we get back the benefit of one cache miss loading 8 (or more) keys. And we only load the full key when the comparison ties.
The same node with inline keys: the first 8 bytes of every key, 64 bytes, one cache line. One compare of all of them leaves a single candidate, and only it is read from the heap.
Pause
What about keys with long prefixes? Many keys, like URLs and paths, have long prefixes. If we just take the first 8 bytes as the inline key, we may compare nothing at all. bbtree addresses this with prefix_keys: the common prefix of all keys in a node9
9Rudolf Bayer and Karl Unterauer, Prefix B-Trees (TODS 1977).
. The beauty of prefix_keys is that no node has to store them. Every key in a node sorts between the two separators on either side of the node in its parent. So if those two separators share their first 20 bytes, every key in the node starts with the same 20 bytes.
Neighboring Wikipedia titles. The parent's two separators share their first 20 bytes, so every key of the child does too. Over the first 8 bytes, the keys all tie; past the shared 20, they all differ.
Pause
So each node only stores the length of its prefix, and keeps the window of each key right after it, which makes inline keys far more effective.
How does this apply to other key types, and how does it work with Rust's type system?
It's clear that String and Vec<u8> benefit from this optimization. But integers like u64 and u128 can too; we just need to mind the endianness: stored big-endian, their bytes sort in the same order as the numbers.
Four keys of one leaf of a tree of 10M random u64s, as bytes: the prefix its separators share, which the leaf skips; the 2 bytes it keeps as each inline key; and the rest, read only on a tie.
For other key types, like compound keys in structs, users can implement the InlineKey trait, and when they do, we use the inline keys wherever we can.
pub trait InlineKey: Ord {
    /// How many bytes of each inline key the nodes keep: 2, 4 or 8.
    const WIDTH: InlineWidth = InlineWidth::Eight;

    /// Bytes `offset..offset + 8` of the key's encoding, big-endian,
    /// zero past its end, which orders as the keys do.
    fn inline_key_at(&self, offset: usize) -> InlineWord;
}

// A compound key, ordered by customer, then order: its encoding is// both fields' bytes, one after the other.#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]struct OrderKey {
    customer: u32,
    order: u32,
}

impl InlineKey for OrderKey {
    fn inline_key_at(&self, offset: usize) -> InlineWord {
        let mut bytes = [0; 16];
        bytes[..4].copy_from_slice(&self.customer.to_be_bytes());
        bytes[4..8].copy_from_slice(&self.order.to_be_bytes());
        let start = offset.min(8);
        u64::from_be_bytes(bytes[start..start + 8].try_into().unwrap())
    }
}

let orders: BBTreeMap<OrderKey, u64, _> =
    BBTreeMap::with_strategy(WithInlineKey);
The trickiest part is Rust's type system. If we required every key type to implement InlineKey, bbtree couldn't be a drop-in replacement for std's BTreeMap/BTreeSet. Nightly Rust has specialization10
10RFC 1210: impl specialization, unstable since 2016 (tracking issue).
for exactly this. For stable Rust, we specialize the common types by hand: u64, i64, u128, i128, String, str, &str, Vec<u8>, &[u8], Box<str>, Box<[u8]>, [u8; 16], [u8; 20] and [u8; 32]. So without any extra work, the built-in types are optimized, and users can still implement the trait for their own types to get the full benefit.
Results
After these optimizations, we can show how many cache lines a lookup touches.
Cache lines brought in from memory per lookup that finds its key, 10M entries, one thread, Ryzen 9 9900X; lower is better.
Bonus: batch mode using Rust's async state machines
So far we have focused on maximizing the value of a cache miss: packing as much information as possible into one cache line.
There's a more advanced optimization: hiding the cost of cache misses.
The simplest way to hide latency is software prefetching: while working on one key, we prefetch the next one. This usually works well, but it isn't enough for B-trees.
This is because a B-tree's memory accesses are fundamentally chained: you don't know which node to fetch next until you have searched the current one.
But B-trees are often read or built in batches, which lets us play a trick with Rust's async state machines. A batch is one call with many keys, such as BBTreeMap's get_many_copied and insert_many: an array of keys in, an array of answers out.
The high-level idea is simple: in Rust we often treat an IO operation as a Future, and await it. In bbtree, we treat a cache miss as a Future, and await it too. Database research has interleaved lookups like this for years, by hand and with coroutines11
11Onur Kocberber, Babak Falsafi and Boris Grot, Asynchronous Memory Access Chaining (VLDB 2015); Georgios Psaropoulos et al., Interleaving with Coroutines: A Practical Approach for Robust Index Joins (VLDB 2017); Christopher Jonathan et al., Exploiting Coroutines to Attack the "Killer Nanoseconds" (VLDB 2018).
.
The code looks roughly like this (they run in a single thread):
fn get_many<const N: usize>(&self, keys: [&K; N]) -> [Option<V>; N] {
    let lanes = keys.map(|key| self.search(key));
    block_on(join_all(lanes))}
And search looks like this:
async fn search(&self, key: &K) -> Option<V> {
    let mut node = self.root();
    while node.is_internal() {
        let edge = node.search(key);
        node = node.child(edge);
        prefetch(node.header()).await;
    }
    node.get(key)}
Four u64 keys looked up together on one core, each key's search a task, from bbtree's own run of the batch; time is counted in turns. In its turn, a task reads the line it prefetched, steps down the tree, prefetches the next line and yields; while that line is on its way, the core runs the other tasks.
Pause
But we need to be very careful:
A cache miss costs 100 ns, so our Future must be as lightweight as possible. This means we can't use tokio or any general-purpose async runtime, because their overhead is already higher than a cache miss. bbtree polls its lanes with a tiny executor of its own: no allocation, no runtime.
Each async function in Rust is a state machine generated at compile time. We want this state machine to be as small as possible, so that switching between states is cheap.
There's no way to know whether a cache line is already in cache, so we have to guess. In bbtree that's not so hard: onc

title: GitHub - Zagitta/gpu-unlock: Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents · GitHub
content:
GPU unlock 1.0.0
Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents
This Linux kernel module combines the CMP unlocker's V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. It runs the unlock, writes the speed selectors (SS0 0x88888888, which selects the full BF16 rate, and the 4-bit SS1 0x8 IMLA4) and performs FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver.
The benefit of this early kmod driver is that it does not require manual patching each time nvidia releases a new driver version.
The effect of this unlock is that it doubles the instruction issuing speed of FP/BF16 FMA into FP32 operations on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards.
3090 Ti dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W, five-sample medians with FP32 accumulation:
Input Before After
FP16 87.46 TFLOPS 118.39 TFLOPS
BF16 87.50 TFLOPS 157.41 TFLOPS
TF32 42.58 TFLOPS 82.61 TFLOPS
Tested cards
Results reported by users. The module accepts every GeForce ID listed in kernel/gpu_unlock/main.c, but the cards below are the ones someone has reported on. Please add yours with a compatibility report, whether it worked or not.
Chip Card PCI ID Result BF16 GEMM gain Reports
GA102 RTX 3090 Ti 10de:2203 Unlocked +68–80% #1
GA102 RTX 3090 10de:2204 Unlocked +25–67% #5, #9, #10, #17, #25, #27, #33
GA102 RTX 3080 Ti 20 GB (OEM, GA102-250) 10de:2205 Unlock completes, BF16 stays at half rate — #28
GA102 RTX 3080 10 GB 10de:2206 Unlocked +70–73% #14
GA102 RTX 3080 20 GB (memory upgrade) 10de:2206 Unlocked +56–59% #10, #15
GA104 RTX 3070 10de:2484 Unlocked +73–81% #10, #12
GA104 RTX 3070 Ti 10de:2482 Not tested with this module (the same unlock worked from a UEFI port on Windows) — #32
GA106 RTX 3060 12 GB 10de:2504 Unlocked about +80% #13, #31
GA103 any 10de:2414 No reports yet — —
The gains are dense GEMM throughput from each report's own benchmark, so they are not directly comparable. The power limit matters a lot: the lowest figure (+25%) is from cards capped at 225 W.
Matrix-heavy work speeds up: LLM prefill (+14–36% in #9, #15, #25 and #33), diffusion and FlashAttention. LLM decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth, and INT8 work stay about the same. The reports that compared outputs found them bit-identical before and after.
Reports also cover up to four cards in one machine, the card driving the display, and cards passed through to a VM with vfio-pci (#17).
How to install
First run:
git clone https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
cd gpu-unlock
make install
Then append gpu_unlock.targets=all to your kernel command line, keeping existing options:
GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint): add it inside GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub, then run sudo update-grub.
GRUB (Arch/CachyOS): same edit, then run sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
Fedora/RHEL: run sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all".
systemd-boot: append it to the options line in your boot entry (bootctl status shows its location).
UKI / generated entries: add it to /etc/kernel/cmdline and regenerate your boot images/entries (e.g. sudo mkinitcpio -P for mkinitcpio UKIs).
Local build
Every build downloads the pinned NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS, checks their SHA-256, and generates firmware only in the build directory and the binary package. All three formats install through the same make install-* targets. Packages are built from the committed HEAD.
Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step (asks for your sudo password):
make install        # detect the distribution and select an installer
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf install
make install uses /etc/os-release (ID, then ID_LIKE) to detect Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, or Fedora/RHEL/CentOS families. The RPM installer requires DNF. For other distributions, select a compatible explicit target above.
make arch, make deb and make rpm only build. Debian and RPM packages go to build/deb and build/rpm. The NVIDIA inputs are cached in ~/.cache/gpu-unlock/inputs (make inputs; override with INPUTS=). dpkg-buildpackage itself never uses the network, so a clean-chroot build (sbuild or pbuilder) needs GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS pointing at that cache. The make dist archive, the Debian source package and the .nosrc.rpm contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware.
Boot flow and opt-in
The packages put gpu_unlock and its firmware in the initramfs and load it there, before nvidia can bind a card:
mkinitcpio: /etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf inserts gpu_unlock right before nvidia in MODULES, so a display card is blank for as short a time as possible. Without nvidia in the image, it goes last and still runs before an nvidia loaded from the root filesystem. Images are rebuilt on install. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image built with -c <config> or a preset _config; put gpu_unlock right before nvidia in that config's MODULES yourself.
initramfs-tools: /usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf.
dracut: /usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf.
With initramfs-tools and dracut, the module is built for every installed kernel that has headers, and those kernels' images are rebuilt on install and again on removal. Kernels installed later get the module and a new image from the kernel's own install hooks.
There is no softdep nvidia pre: rule: kmod honours only the first softdep nvidia line it reads, so other packages' rules (nvidia-utils, gddr6_hwmon) would silently override it, or it would override theirs.
The module does nothing unless the kernel command line opts in:
gpu_unlock.targets=all                          # every unbound GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0                 # only these cards
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0,0000:22:00.0    # comma-separated
Addresses are full PCI names as lspci -D prints them (hex digits in either case), independent of GPU numbering and display role. An entry that is not a GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card, including all mixed with addresses, is logged and ignored. The cards are unlocked concurrently, about a second in all however many there are, and each on its own: a card that is already bound or powered down is skipped. Bus mastering that the board firmware left on (Supermicro X11 does this whatever its option ROM and bus master settings) is cleared first; a card some driver already initialised is still refused. Then nvidia loads and binds every card as usual.
The display card works too. Its firmware framebuffer (the boot console and Plymouth) keeps running while the unlock's firmware steps run, and is removed just before the card's reset, as nvidia-drm would do a moment later anyway. Its screen is blank from that reset until nvidia-drm takes over.
Loading the module by hand after boot does nothing to a card that nvidia has bound.
Suspend to RAM powers the cards off, which resets the speed selectors. After resume the module unlocks every card it unlocked at boot again, before nvidia resumes it: its suspend notifier runs just ahead of the one nvidia resumes its cards from (NVreg_UseKernelSuspendNotifiers=1, the default in current drivers; nvidia-resume.service runs later still). This adds about a second to resume. A card that kept power, as in suspend to idle, is still unlocked and is only read. A card that nvidia has already resumed, or that is bound to another driver, is left as it is, and the log says why. Add gpu_unlock.resume=0 to the kernel command line, or write 0 to /sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume, to turn this off. Hibernation is not covered.
Check the result with:
journalctl -k -b | grep gpu_unlock
lspci -nnk -s 0000:21:00.0
To stop unlocking, remove gpu_unlock.targets= from the kernel command line; for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.
If the firmware on a card never stops, the module logs it and keeps the DMA buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off before trying again.
The kernel module and local packaging are GPL-2.0-only. The generated payload derives from the pinned CMP reference; NVIDIA firmware remains under its own terms. See firmware/NOTICE.md and licenses/ for attribution and notices.

Movie News
Xbox Turns Down Netflix $500 Million Offer
By Garth Franklin
Saturday, October 24th 2026 5:20 pm
Halo Studios, Microsoft
Netflix reportedly offered Microsoft $500 million for a seven year deal that would allow the streaming giant to adapt shows and films about Xbox characters.
Puck broke the news, indicating that Microsoft responded with an offer for $800 million – as a result, the deal has reportedly fallen through.
In a statement to Puck, Xbox said, “We have received record-breaking interest in our I.P.; Netflix is a valued partner and we are excited for the forthcoming release of our Minecraft and Diablo animated series together, among other adaptations.”
Microsoft is now said to be in pursit of “smaller deals with more partners,” doing things on a case-by-case basis rather than an overarching exclusivity deal.
Microsoft previously partnered with Paramount to produce the live-action “Halo” series, which ran for two seasons. They currently have a “Call of Duty” film in the works at Paramount, a third season of “Fallout” at Amazon and a sequel to “A Minecraft Movie” opening next year.
Titles like “Gears of War,” “The Elder Scrolls” and “Sea of Thieves” are also being pitched for possible adaptations.
Netflix has various works based on games coming out, including the animated “Cyberpunk: Edgerunners” which returned this week.

title: GitHub - slee-persis/GVS5H: GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard | Fable 5 Level Coding for a Fifth the Price - or on a Single GPU · GitHub
content:
GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
GVS5H: Gorilla vs. 5 Humans
Results
Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend.
Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.
— the paper
Running the code
Needs uv and an API key for the model you want to test.
cd codebase/v2-current
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...

LCB_RELEASE=release_v6 \
ESCALATION_CLOUD_MAX_TOKENS=128000 \
ESCALATION_CLOUD_TIMEOUT=7200 \
MULTIAGENT_MODEL=openai:gpt-5.6-terra \
uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with 'datasets<4' --with numpy --with anthropic \
  python escalation/run_bench.py --engine multiagent --only lcb --lcb 100 --parallel 8
--engine multiagent runs the manager; --engine single is the one-call baseline.
Other models: anthropic:<model>, dashscope:<model>, openrouter:<model>, each with its own *_API_KEY.
The pass@1 score prints at the end. Results are written to runs/results.json, workspaces to runs/ws/.
License

title: “We should be more ambitious with the software we build”
content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying
[W]e should be more ambitious1 with the software we build
There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader2, this money overflow bug, etc.
This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free3, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.
That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).
As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.
But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.
If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.
Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:
Ripgrep
Compiling Rust
Syscall and filesystem overhead
At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind).
For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.
My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now4.
Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.
When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher)5.
For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats6.
BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle7. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing8. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.
Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.
I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.
I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that woudl be a super interestin thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago.
Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build
Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):
If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think
I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover
My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.
And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with this (although it can speed up implementation once you have a clean spec), but for that, I was able to set up some kind of janky set of consistency checks between all of the inconsistent explanations of the game rules, which got fairly cl

title: How Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
content:
OCT 22 2026
How we deploy Trillion-parameter frontier models on Cerebras
SARAH CHIENG
One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.
In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.
We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.
By the end, you'll understand:
How we fit the full model into on-chip memory
How we map the model across multiple chips
How we handle a high # of concurrent requests
Breaking it down with Kimi K3
Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.
It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here.
For this illustrative example, we use:
A 256k assumed average request size
4-bit weight quantization (like the Hugging Face implementation)
An 8-bit KV cache
#1: Size of Each layer
To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer.
Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is:
Dividing that payload by 93 layers then gives:
#2: Number of Wafers
Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type:
Dense layers need additional room for a KV cache, because each dense (full-attention) layer stores the keys and values for every token in every active request. So, we place one dense layer per wafer and leave the remaining SRAM for its KV cache.
Linear-attention layers do not require additional room for a KV cache. Instead of storing keys and values for every token, a linear-attention layer keeps a small, fixed-size state per request, regardless of context length. That leaves room for two linear layers per wafer (2 × 16 GB = 32 GB).
Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers, we get:
This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers.
#3: Connecting the wafers together
Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.
It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.
This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.
#4: How we serve 1 request
Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.
For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.
#5: How we serve many requests
This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?
No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.
While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.

To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.
#6: How many requests can we serve?
The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.
For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with:
Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case:
Calculating the # of Concurrent Requests
To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up:
To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide:
The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously.
Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed.
How this scales beyond 3T parameters
The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.

AI and the Fall? of the Creative Class
America is Losing Hundreds of Thousands of Jobs in Media, Film & the Arts. How Much is AI to Blame?
JOSEPH POLITANO
SEP 27, 2026
268
58
52
Share
Thanks for reading! If you haven’t subscribed, please click the button below:
Subscribe
By subscribing, you’ll join over 80,000 people who read Apricitas!
America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone. That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008. Yet there’s no generalized recession today—instead, this period of job loss coincides with the rise of AI systems that can compose wholesale novels, photorealistic images, soundalike music, and practically every other form of digital art, en masse and at extremely low costs. Is this the fall of the Creative Class?
Proving the exact amount of AI-driven job loss in the arts is extremely difficult. Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights. The effects of AI are also hard to disentangle from other factors currently affecting arts businesses, like consolidation in Hollywood, offshoring of content production, or the continued displacement of traditional media providers in favor of social media creators. Yet perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.
Some of those digital job losses are just a continuation of prior trends, like in the publishing industry where technological change has been continually grinding away newspaper and magazine jobs for decades. Yet for sectors like live broadcasting, streaming, or graphic design, recent experience is an unusual downturn compared to the tranquility of years prior. Then there’s the worst-hit sector, movie & sound recording, which has been bleeding jobs at a nearly unprecedented pace over the last three years.
Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total. At the depths touched this summer, total employment was lower than at any point since the 2008 recession and approaching the lowest point in 30 years. The streaming era has proven an extremely difficult transition, with traditional films and TV shows losing watch time to user-generated and increasingly AI-assisted or AI-generated content flows.
Overall, nearly half the media job losses of the last four years have been concentrated in the movie & sound recording sector that includes Hollywood. Written publishing has been the next-largest source of job loss, with employment down by more than 70k over the same time frame. Yet the job losses have by no means been contained to any particular part of media; instead they’ve hit nearly every subsector at some point. Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months. Will further AI development continue displacing workers in creative industries?
Subscribe
Can the Arts Business Model Survive?
To understand what could happen to the business of art amidst the rise of AI, it’s important to understand what did happen to it during the first digital transition, the rise of the internet.
It was the turn of the millennium, and Metallica had a problem. Demos of their upcoming, unreleased tracks were bouncing around radio and the internet, originally leaked onto a new internet file-sharing website called Napster. There they found thousands of files shared amongst hundreds of thousands of users, many of which were direct rips of albums that sold for $15 being offered for free. The most anticipated albums were often leaked online even before they were on store shelves. Metallica sued Napster for copyright infringement, and they were soon joined by separate suits from other prominent artists and eventually the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).
Much of the general public was understandably unsympathetic to Metallica, perceived as a bunch of already-successful millionaires trying to bilk even more money from listeners, and were even less sympathetic towards the RIAA, perceived as scurrilous middlemen who take from artists and fans alike. But the two of them easily won their lawsuit, forcing Napster into bankruptcy. Yet Metallica may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.
The modern internet made file-sharing extremely easy, and no matter how much whac-a-mole companies played, they could not possibly catch every illegal upload. The perennial threat of piracy undermined their copyright and limited their ability to charge for music. Eventually, the value of individual songs fell to the point that companies like Spotify and Apple Music could swoop in to acquire massive catalogues, consolidate them, and charge a comparatively trivial fee for access. For what a single Metallica album would have cost in 2000, you can now get a month’s worth of unlimited access to nearly all human-made music.
The music industry has never returned to the heyday paydays of the peak CD era—even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales. This was a massive boon to consumers, but it was also a squeeze on musicians that forced them to fundamentally change their business model over time. Instead of just selling records to earn money directly, music itself increasingly became a loss-leading advertisement for the live concerts (and merch) that provided a growing share of artists’ income. Tours got longer, venues got bigger, ticket prices skyrocketed, and musicians frequently took on roles closer to public influencers than isolated artistes. Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.
Of course, there were still significant downsides to the transition into the streaming era. Bands (especially smaller ones) complain about the unending pressure to always be on tour. Musicians whose content was suited to home listening lost out to those more suited to giant festivals. Even accounting for concert revenues, musicians made less money than before. Yet musicians fared better than many areas of entertainment subsectors because there was a live component to fall back on—for many media industries, the digital era left no such comfort.
Over time, the business of video has moved in the opposite direction of music—out of the theatre and into the home. Hollywood formerly made most of its money enticing customers to visit sold-out movie theatres, but these were gradually supplanted by broadcast TV, cable, and physical media. Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval. That is, until the modern streaming era.
Today, the plethora of video options and the rise of social media have sent video producers into a vicious competition for limited attention. Even before adjusting for inflation, movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop. The mountain of free user-generated content on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, or social media was already presenting harsh competition for traditional video companies in the years before ChatGPT’s launch, and now streaming services are also competing with a flood of AI-generated content. The business model of video media is fundamentally getting squeezed, and unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.
The actual worst-case scenario for creative workers amidst the AI revolution is something similar to what happened to the publishing industry after the advent of the internet—that is, near-total collapse of their fundamental business model. Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping. Magazine publishers likewise have let 66% of their staff go since the 90s, while book publishers have lost 40%.
The routine informational updates that previously formed newspapers’ bread-and-butter were all de-bundled—box scores moved to sports websites, stock movements went to financial websites, forecasts went to weather websites—each loss compounding on itself to undermine consumers’ need to buy the paper. Search engines became the first place people looked to for information, and newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead. The collective of social media users became faster at breaking any news story than a daily paper could ever hope to be. When papers eventually did start aggressively paywalling content, the internet made it trivially easy for people to just copy the articles’ content and share it beyond the paywall. The entire business model had collapsed, to the point that now only a select few major newspapers can even survive.
That scale of copyright dilution and forced unbundling is the worst-case scenario for media businesses in the age of AI. It’s possible arts jobs could survive via consumers’ deep-seated aversion to explicitly AI-generated content, but AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer. Roughly 32% of workers in the overall arts, entertainment, and recreation sector use Generative AI to some extent, which is less than the 62% average across all industries, but still enough that virtually every major media project could have some AI within its workflow.
Indeed, AI is likely seeping into media production processes in ways large companies themselves would struggle to prevent even when they desire to—how can a TV studio be sure nobody in their writers’ room is consulting ChatGPT for jokes or any storyboard artist is generating concept art? And even if professional TV and movie studios do effectively hold out against temptation and prevent internal AI use, how long can they compete with the large mass of wannabe independent creators with much fewer scruples? Plenty of media businesses tried to hold out against the algorithmic content waves of the 2010s and were buried as a result.
Subscribe
Conclusions
Yet fundamentally, it’s difficult to meaningfully predict how new technologies will interact with existing arts businesses. Take the unexpected resurgence in book sales over the last four years. The novel as a commercial art form had been struggling for decades, with fewer books sold in 2019 than at the beginning of the millennium, but the last six years have seen an unprecedented 70% surge in sales. The unlikely savior of the printed word came from perhaps its polar opposite—TikTok.
Of course, fewer people read now than ever before—for the general public, short-form video apps have accelerated the displacement of reading, just as TV, video games, or social media before them. Yet for a dwindling number of dedicated repeat readers, “BookTok” became a new way to source reviews, analysis, discourse, and community in a way that boosted the reading experience and absolutely turbocharged book sales. It’s possible that AI tools could have those same totally unpredictable spillovers for other museums, concerts, or other forms of art in ways that are unpredictable today, in much the same way short-form video saved books in ways that could never have been anticipated beforehand.
At the end of the day, the arts are only a small sector of the overall macroeconomy. Media made up a small share of the labor market even at its peak, and it has always been difficult to get hired in creative industries to the point that making fun of art students’ job prospects became an easy punchline. The movie industry has an income profile closer to eggs or bicycles than something major like healthcare or finance. Were the goal to create art for art’s sake, for the intangible and nonmonetizable cultural benefits, it would be relatively easy to counterbalance any economic impacts of AI on artists just by reversing recent cuts to the National Endowments for the Arts & Humanities.
It’s telling that Anthropic, the most prominent AI lab, has basically never bothered with image, video, or music generation, because the prospective economic benefits are marginal when compared to using AI to tackle math or scientific problems. OpenAI learned this lesson the hard way when it was forced to abandon its video generation platform Sora, deciding it had better use for its limited compute than making synthetic TikToks. Nowadays, the art generation is done primarily by secondary players running smaller models, though even these are large enough to threaten significant disruption to legacy media businesses.
In other words, the primary impacts of AI art will be on culture and society rather than the macroeconomy. Yet arts jobs might be a microcosm for other “creative-adjacent” work that occupies a much larger share of economic activity. Take the tech sector itself, which is the clearest place where AI-driven job loss has shown up outside the media business, as powerful coding agents replace human programmers. Annual tech job gains stood at nearly 300k in 2022, but the sector has been bleeding jobs every year since then in what is now its longest labor market downturn.
Right now, AI-driven job displacement has been relatively minor outside of these few narrow sectors. Unemployment is higher than it was four years ago but still below even the 2010s average, and overall job turnover rates remain extremely low. Some white-collar sectors that looked prime for AI automation have even been on a hiring spree over the last few years, including legal and engineering firms. Yet if the economic impact of AI ends up being anywhere near large enough to validate the trillions of dollars investors are currently betting on it, these economic disruptions will only spread from here.
