2026 May 24, 10:29

I feel you, on one hand we cant go back, on the other, we have
to go back. Im not sure where that leaves us. All I know is that
I (myself) need to slow down. - y4my4m

title: I Built a Stereo Vision Board for Hardware Hackers - Rootkit Labs Blog
content:
This article was written entirely by a human, for humans.
I tend to get excited about certain chips. This time, it was a microprocessor: The Rockchip RV1103 is a single-core 1.1 GHz ARM Cortex-A7 SoC (system on chip) with 64 MB of DDR2 RAM and a MIPI CSI-2 bus shoved into a QFN-88 package. With this chip, I built a cheap, simple stereo vision board with built-in compute and Linux support.
Design Files
I envision integrating this board into robotics projects, like an Arduino needing obstacle avoidance or navigation. Once powered up, the board transmits data over serial. Or you can use it on its own, with everything you’d expect from a Linux board.
The video below shows image capture and depth processing on the hardware:
This blog post outlines the hardware, firmware, and software details!
System Overview
The PCB
A cheap four-layer board worked for this project.
Top Layer: Controlled-impedance traces: USB, MIPI, and Ethernet. With some Signal/Power.
Inner L1: Solid ground.
Inner L2: Signal/Power
Bottom Layer: Signal/Power
I got the board mostly correct on the first shot, but there were a few issues:
I requested the wrong SoC. That was a fun replacement.
The holes for the lens mounts were drilled at 1.8 mm instead of 2.2 mm.
1k resistors were too small to make the LEDs light up nicely.
The 0.9 V trace was too thin, although it seemed to work fine.
The Kernel, Bootloader, and OS
I needed a bootable OS, with drivers, a bootloader and a kernel. For this I used my favorite Linux build system: Buildroot. Buildroot combines these elements into sdcard.img, which you flash to an SD card, pop into the board, and boot.
Sadly, not everything needed for this project is available upstream. The Rockchip MIPI drivers, hardware accelerators, and some other key components all came from the vendor BSP. Buildroot has support for out-of-tree kernels.
For this chip, there are a few different boot stages. Most ARM MPUs look something like this:
(Bootloader) BootROM: Gets TPL and runs it. This is in ROM and uses SRAM (smaller, non-main RAM).
(Bootloader) TPL (“Tertiary Program Loader”): Sets up the DRAM controller. This is a binary from Rockchip.
(Bootloader) SPL (“Secondary Program Loader”): Loads U-Boot, bundled with the U-Boot project.
(Bootloader) U-Boot: This is our main bootloader; it loads the kernel. It has other fancy features.
(Kernel): Linux
(OS) Init System: Starts services.
After some simple config in Buildroot, I had access to a shell over serial. I eventually moved to SSH, with the USB-C port as an Ethernet adapter.
The Software Stack
The software MVP needed to communicate with the kernel to get image data, control the camera, and use the hardware accelerators. Luckily, everything in the kernel space marked above was assembled for us with Buildroot. We just needed to make the blue part, but I’ll explain the rest briefly.
Kernel Space
You may notice drivers get more abstract at the top of the diagram, while lower down they’re hardware specific. This means a user application can talk to a node created by V4L2 and doesn’t need to care about specific camera commands.
There are SoC-specific drivers for the SoC peripherals (like I2C, CSI, etc.). This is so the camera driver (OV9281 in our case) doesn’t need to know which SoC it’s running on.
This is all pretty standard Linux device driver stuff, so I won’t go into any more details beyond this.
User Space
The data eventually flows up to Video4Linux2, which exposes our cameras in various nodes /dev/videoX. Each camera shows 11 video nodes:
video0: Normal video capture
video1-3: Other stream IDs
video4-7: Scalers
video8-10: Auxiliary tools
Camera control is exposed through /dev/v4l-subdevX. We can use these nodes to set exposure and control various camera features.
The “Rockchip Video Engine” is exposed through /dev/rve. We use the proprietary librve.a to talk with the engine and schedule various hardware video acceleration tasks. I’ll get more into this later.
The userspace app…
Configures the cameras from /dev/v4l-subdevX
Takes the image data from /dev/videoX
Feeds it into the /dev/rve node
The Rockchip Video Engine contains a SAD engine (sum of absolute differences). This is a hardware accelerator block that runs on the Rockchip SoC itself.
SAD is the core of how we do stereoscopic vision. A grayscale image can be represented as a matrix, with each element being a number from 0 to 255. Let’s say we have 2x images that are 2 × 2 px each. We can calculate the SAD:
Image 1  Image 2  Absolute differences
[10  20] [10  20] [0  0]
[30  40] [30  40] [0  0]

SAD = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0
We can say the two images are the same.
Now instead of comparing these tiny images, we have two big images and break them up into a bunch of smaller images, called patches, and do this everywhere.
Normalized SAD per patch (0 = identical).
We now have an algorithm to determine how similar patches of the image are, so with this information we can certainly say that this section of this image is different.
SAD-based stereo block matching uses the same principle, but compares a vertical column of patches after a horizontal shift. Our two images come from two separate cameras, separated horizontally by a distance we call the baseline. We keep one image fixed, shift the other, and try to find matching blocks; when the blocks match, this is a depth value. If they match at a very early shift, this is a far-away value, while a later shift is a closer image.
Stereo images: Middlebury Cones.
You can see that images farther away require less shifting to get a match, and once you get a match, the shifting required is your depth! The boxes show your patch size, and the green box is showing a SAD match. This is illustrated in this GIF above with three separate depths.
What’s Next?
I would like to sell a few of these devices and get some feedback.
If you’re interested in this device, please sign up for the email notification here. If I get more than 20 signups, I’ll order another 10 boards with all the fixes and list these for sale. Please note this isn’t a pre-order, but only sign up if you are serious about supporting the project :)
If I get enough interest, the next stage of the project will be software cleanups, image optimisations, implementing SLAM, and YOLO.
Thanks for reading!
Author
Ryan Walker

title: In Rainbows
content:
In Rainbows
Written 2026-10-06
rainbows is a specification for devices connected to the ok virtual machine, named after Radiohead's album In Rainbows. ok itself only provides instruction evaluation and the "data" and "return" stacks for basic computation, but if you wanted to output something to a screen or a console, or receive input from a mouse or keyboard, you'd have to "map" those devices into memory.
Memory Mapping
ok calls ok_mem_read(addr) whenever it needs to read a byte from RAM, and ok_mem_write(addr) whenever it needs to write a byte to RAM. These are functions that you define yourself, in order to make user-defined memory-mapping possible. For example, with no memory-mapping, your definition of ok_mem_read might look like this:
// assuming "ram" is defined as an array of bytes elsewhere
uint8_t ok_mem_read(size_t address) {
  return ram[address];
}
But, let's say you want to be able to read data from a console's standard input (stdin). You could map a "magic" location in RAM so that reading a byte from this address reads data from stdin, like so:
#define STDIN_MAGIC (3)

uint8_t ok_mem_read(size_t address) {
  if (address == STDIN_MAGIC) {
    char ch;
    read(STDIN_FILENO, &ch, 1);
    return (uint8_t)ch;
  }

  return ram[address];
}
With this, reading a value from RAM at this address (in ok's assembly language, that might look like #000003 lod1) will read a byte from stdin.
The idea behind rainbows is that it defines these magic values for you, in order to provide a standard set of input/output devices for someone to use- turning ok into a proper "fantasy computer" rather than just a stack-based instruction evaluator.
Devices
rainbows is still actively being written, so these descriptions for the devices it supports may become outdated rather soon (but I'll try to update this page if I change something).
As of right now, I've either implemented or have plans to implement the following devices (in order of how confident I am in their current definition):
RbConsole, for interfacing with a POSIX-style CLI
RbArith, for providing more convenient math operations that ok doesn't support very well on its own
RbDisk, for providing disk I/O and persistent storage
RbDatetime, for providing date/time information
RbScreen, for providing a screen/framebuffer
Now, we'll go over the memory layout I have for the devices I've implemented so far, as well as any thoughts I have for the devices that I'm still unsure about. Expect the memory addresses described below to change as I work on rainbows more!
RbConsole
RbConsole uses the following addresses- the numbers on the left side of the table are the addresses, and the text on the right side of the table are the "names" of those addresses that the device uses (think of them like struct fields):
|---------------------|
|      RbConsole      |
|--------+------------|
| 000000 | stdin (R)  |
|--------+------------|
| 000001 | stdout (W) |
|--------+------------|
| 000002 | argc (R)   |
|--------+------------|
| 000003 | arg_index  |
|--------+------------|
| 000004 | arg_char_i |
|--------+------------|
| 000005 | arg_char   |
|--------+------------|
Reading a byte from stdin, of course, reads from stdin, and writing a byte to stdout does exactly what you'd expect it to.
argc stores the number of command line arguments that were provided (like argc in C).
From here it gets interesting- if you want to read a specific command line argument, you first write a value to arg_index to determine which command line argument you're looking at (0-indexed, of course). Then, you write a value to arg_char_i to determine which character of the argument at arg_index you're looking at, and then reading a byte from arg_char reads that character, and will read 0 if you're at the end or out of bounds.
So, reading a byte from arg_char is a bit like doing this (in C):
char* argument = argv[arg_index];
uint8_t arg_char = argument[arg_char_i];
It's a bit clunky, but the alternative ideas that I had were either to be able to store an argument at a specific location in memory by writing that location into a place in the RbConsole device (which would mean RbConsole could manipulate any arbitrary place in memory, which I didn't like), or it would've meant that RbConsole would need a buffer with a predefined length to store an individual argument, which I didn't wanna do since I wasn't sure what a good predefined length would be (plus I didn't feel like having some kind of error handling for if an argument was too long to fit in the buffer).
This device, as of right now, is fully implemented!
RbArith
RbArith adds support for multiplication, division, and modulo, for 1, 2, 3, and 4-byte unsigned integers. Here is its memory layout:
|-----------------|
|     RbArith     |
|--------+--------|
| 000006 | op     |
|--------+--------|
| 000007 | err    |
|--------+--------|
| 000008 | width  |
|--------+--------|
| 000009 | x      |
| 00000a |        |
| 00000b |        |
| 00000c |        |
|--------+--------|
| 00000d | y      |
| 00000e |        |
| 00000f |        |
| 000010 |        |
|--------+--------|
| 000011 | result |
| 000012 |        |
| 000013 |        |
| 000014 |        |
|--------+--------|
When you write a magic value to op, the operation associated with that value is performed on x and y, with the result being stored in result. When this operation is performed, x, y, and result are treated as having a width of width - 1 (so 3 treats them as 4-byte values, 2 as 3-byte values, 1 as 2-byte values, and 0 as 1-byte values). The values that op can take on are as follows:
0 is a no-op, no operation is performed.
1 stores x * y into result
2 stores x / y into result, setting err to 1 if y is 0
3 stores x % y into result, setting err to 2 if y is 0
I may add other math operations (or perhaps random number generation?) in the future. If/when I do, I'll just add them as new values that op could take on (5, 6, etc).
RbDisk
RbDisk provides disk I/O using a library I wrote recently, which I talk more about in my "Playing with Blocks" article.
RbDisk's memory layout is as follows:
|----------------------------|
|           RbDisk           |
|--------+-------------------|
| 000015 | capacity          |
| 000016 |                   |
| 000017 |                   |
| 000018 |                   |
|--------+-------------------|
| 000019 | update            |
|--------+-------------------|
| 00001a | error             |
|--------+-------------------|
| 00001b | current           |
| 00001c |                   |
| 00001d |                   |
| 00001e |                   |
|--------+-------------------|
| 00001f | data (1024 bytes) |
| ...    |                   |
| 00041e |                   |
|--------+-------------------|
When you run the emulator for rainbows, you provide a BlockFile (described in more detail in the article I mentioned earier) or can choose to create a new one. This file has a set capacity, i.e. a max number of 1024-byte "blocks" that are stored within it. This value is stored in capacity.
Note: if/when I ever decide to get rainbows running on bare-metal (without an underlying OS), rather than using a BlockFile, it would just use the free space of the disk itself.
You can then read a value from update to load the contents of the block at index current into data. Writing a value to update will then store data to the block at index current.
RbDatetime
This device I'm still unsure about- the idea behind RbDatetime is that it provides clock/date info, but I'm not sure exactly how complex I want it to be. I thought about taking inspiration from (i.e. basically stealing) how Varvara's datetime device works, and just have addresses in memory that store the current year, day, day of the week, hours, minutes, seconds, whether we're in daylight savings time, etc:
But I've also considered just storing the 64-bit Unix time (i.e. the number of "non-leap" seconds since midnight of January 1st, 1970, UTC), and just writing software that determines the date using this information- although this wouldn't be super convenient, considering that ok only supports a maximum integer width of 32 bits. Some systems still store Unix time as a 32-bit value, but this would mean that the value would overflow in early 2038, which is a bit too soon for me to justify using it.
Plus, there's the issue of representing smaller units of time like milliseconds, which may be nice to have depending on what I want to make.
All in all, this device is still a work-in-progress. When I add it though, I have a feeling I'll put it before the RbDisk device, meaning that the addresses for the table above would need to be updated.
RbScreen
This is another device that I'm rather unsure about.
For one thing, I don't know how many colors I'd like to support- Varvara uses 2-bit color, allowing for a maximum of 4 different colors, but I've thought about adding a way to set the "color mode" for the screen. For smaller color depth values, like 1, 2, 4, and 5-bit color, they may be able to set a palette, whereas for larger values, I've considered adding support for 8-bit color (perhaps using RGB332, using 3 bits for "red", 3 bits for "green", and two for "blue"), as well as 16-bit "high" color (using RGB565), and maybe even 24-bit "true" color.
However, for larger color depth values and larger screen resolutions, the memory usage grows rather large. For example, a 1024x600 screen using 24-bit color would have a framebuffer that takes up 1800 kibibytes (where a kibibyte is 1024 bytes) of memory, i.e. around 11% of the total memory that ok can access.
Screen resolution itself is a whole other problem- do I want to allow the user to define the screen size themselves? This would allow for resizable windows, which would be nice for running rainbows as just a program on your system, but then I'd need to have something like a framebuffer_addr field in the section of memory for RbScreen, pointing to where the framebuffer starts, and then any software targeting rainbows would have to account for that (i.e. try not to accidentally overwrite that section of memory during computation).
This brings up other concerns too- for instance, possible support for multiple buffering.
If I didn't allow for a resizable screen/window, I'd then need to decide what resolution I'd want to have, as well as what aspect ratio I'd want. Right now, one of my main goals is to get rainbows running bare-metal on a little laptop I call my zen machine (which I haven't written about yet, but I will eventually). This laptop has a resolution of 1024x600 pixels, which is a bit nonstandard (it's not really 16:9 or 4:3). I've also debated using a 4:3 aspect ratio (perhaps 640x480), mostly just because I like 4:3 a lot, but then running rainbows full-screen may look weird on a 16:9 display.
As you can see, RbScreen is a device that I've thought a lot about, and still haven't really come to a specific solution that I like. At this point it's literally keeping me up at night, and has been since I was first writing about ok.
Other ideas for devices
In terms of other devices I'd like to define/implement eventually, I've thought a bit about an RbKeyboard device for reading keyboard input (perhaps using something like a circular character buffer to track multiple keypresses at once?). Ideally, RbKeyboard would also support some "controller" functionality, like how Varvara's "controller" device supports both keyboard keys as well as treating certain keys (like ctrl, alt, shift, and home) as though they were keys on a Nintendo device (i.e. A, B, Select, and Start). I've debated only using a certain subset of the keyboard, as I quite like using a 60% or 75% keyboard layout.
Another device I've strongly considered is RbFloat, a device for working with 32-bit floating point values, although ideally this device shouldn't be that "essential" for running programs on rainbows (as perhaps I may try to get rainbows software running on a system that doesn't exactly adhere to, or doesn't even use, the 32-bit floating point standard).
Something of note is that I haven't really thought about a "mouse" device- personally, I don't really like using a mouse or trackpad of any kind, so I haven't prioritized making a device for one. I'll definitely implement one eventually, but I want to (somehow) encourage software written for rainbows to be keyboard first, i.e. all software running on rainbows should be perfectly usable with no mouse or pointing device at all. This is especially important for working with the zen machine, since even though it does have a trackpad, it's very small, and the left-click button is broken beyond repair (and I can't find much info about replacement parts or how to repair it in general).
I also haven't really thought much about supporting audio, as I feel like this would be quite the rabbit hole (do I support audio synthesis? Audio samples? MIDI? Some combination of the three? Or maybe I could make my own audio format...).
I haven't considered a networking device for similar reasons- although I have thought about adding a device that basically acts as a very-barebones Gemini protocol client, since I like using Gemini a lot.
Conclusions
As you can see, even though I've been actively working on rainbows for a while, it's still got a long way to go. I first started sketching ideas for it back when I wrote my undergraduate thesis on ok, where originally I had considered implementing rainbows for the latter-half of the thesis rather than attempting to implement a compiler. I quickly realized that just writing a specification for it was a hell of an undertaking, let alone implementing it.
As of right now, my goal is to at least get RbConsole, RbDisk, and RbArith fully implemented, and then from there I may work on a simple compiled language (POP-2000, anyone?) to test their functionality and start writing some "useful" software for rainbows before moving on.
In the meantime, I'll keep this article up-to-date whenever some new developments occur, and I hope you enjoyed listening to me ramble about the rabbit hole that this project has taken me down.

title: Social dynamics of toxic metal industry in medieval Europe: Peak District lead production, AD 600–1500 | Antiquity | Cambridge Core
content:
Introduction
The production of key metals, such as silver and lead, has long been studied by historians of the European Middle Ages (c. AD 400–1500) but textual sources on the origins of these industries are partial and fragmented, providing only hints as to when specialist production may have begun. Over the past two decades, high-resolution palaeoenvironmental studies from lake-, peat- and ice-cores have identified when lead aerosol pollution began to contaminate the environment of northern, western and Mediterranean Europe yet most of these environmental records are derived from areas far from medieval lead- and silver-producing centres (Loveluck et al.
Reference Loveluck
2020). Studies of the impact of pollution in the regions that housed the largest of these medieval metal industries are extremely rare (e.g. Kempter & Frenzel
Reference Kempter and Frenzel
2000), and analyses of the impact of lead pollution on the communities that mined and smelted the metal are all but absent.
Lead (Pb) is a toxic metal that can affect the nervous, renal and reproductive systems when ingested (Farmer et al.
Reference Farmer
2024). Those working with lead during the medieval period would have been exposed to harm at different stages of the mining and smelting processes; for example, through inhalation/ingestion of gases or dust. Once in the body, lead is preferentially deposited in the hard tissues—bone, dentine and enamel. Thus, analysis of lead concentrations (in parts per million (ppm)) in tooth enamel may provide a means to differentiate between individuals who were actively involved with lead mining and processing and those exposed to background levels of pollution from the broader landscape.
This article presents the first analysis of levels of lead contamination among communities living in one of western Europe’s largest lead-producing regions during the Middle Ages: the Derbyshire Peak District, at the southernmost extent of the Pennine hills in central England. It provides the first absolute dates for post-Roman lead production in the region, from the mid-seventh century; with large-scale production contaminating the local environment around certain centres, such as Castleton, by the mid-eighth century (Figure 1). The results further shed light on the age and gender dynamics of seventh- to fifteenth-century lead production, reflecting childhood exposure (between the ages of four and 12 years) and suggesting an association between high lead burden and premature death, especially among women. Comparison with Neolithic to Industrial Revolution populations provides a benchmark of expected lead levels among silver-lead-producer communities in medieval Europe and other periods.
Figure 1.
Locations of places discussed in the text: a) Britain and north-west Europe; b) detail of places in the English East Midlands (figure by A. Bloxam & C.P. Loveluck).
Peak District lead production to AD 1500
Despite evidence for copper mining at Ecton Hill in the Peak District from c. 1880–1640 BC (Timberlake
Reference Timberlake
2017: 714), the first evidence for intentional lead extraction, indicated by a lead casting-model for a socketed axe from Mam Tor (Guilbert
Reference Guilbert
1996) and a lead object from Gardom’s Edge (Barnatt & Smith
Reference Barnatt and Smith
2004: 49), dates from a millennium later. Following Roman annexation of the Peak, lead ingots indicate that large-scale production ensued at c. AD 80–200 (Branigan
Reference Branigan, Hodges and Smith
1991: 60), under a franchise known as the sociorum Lutud(arensium) (Dool & Hughes
Reference Dool and Hughes
1976: 16). Lead production continued among rural communities through the third and fourth centuries, reflected at Carsington, Bradwell, Rainster Rocks and Chee Tor (Branigan
Reference Branigan, Hodges and Smith
1991: 60). Southern Pennines lead, probably from the Peak District, was still arriving in middle Rhine centres such as Cologne and Trier in AD 300–400, formed into coffins and other artefacts (Durali-Mueller et al.
Reference Durali-Mueller
2007: 1566), after which it has been assumed that production largely collapsed, serving only sporadic local needs.
The sudden wealth of mid-seventh-century cemeteries in the Peak District might reflect renewed lead production to resource Christian church building (Loveluck
Reference Loveluck, Bintliff and Hamerow
1995: 90; Figure 2). Smelting of fresh metal has previously been dated only to sometime between c. AD 760 and 860, based on lead isotope analysis of weights from Birka, Sweden (Ambrosiani
Reference Ambrosiani
2013; Kershaw & Merkel
Reference Kershaw and Merkel
2023: 275). However, a charter summary attributed to AD 835 also records a nobleman, Humberht, paying rent for an estate in Wirksworth (Low/White Peak; see Figure 1b) to the monastery at Repton (Derbyshire) in the medium of lead. He was obliged to organise transport of the lead to Canterbury, presumably via the River Humber and the North Sea coast (Kelly & Brooks
Reference Kelly and Brooks
2013: 636–38). This route is mirrored in lead objects and working debris found at eighth-to-ninth-century settlements from Flixborough, Beverley, Riby and Fishtoft (Loveluck
Reference Loveluck
2007: 102–103; Taylor
Reference Taylor and Cope-Faulkner
2012: 70–72; Figure 1). Pewter fittings on the Gokstad ship, Norway (Figure 1a), alloyed using metal from the Peak District/Pennines and Melle (Deux-Sèvres), France, also suggest continued production or recycling of lead from the Peak District into the tenth century (Pedersen et al.
Reference Pedersen
2016: 158–59). Radiocarbon dating of the individuals included in our study provides the first absolute dates for lead production in these centuries through in-vivo contamination concentrations in the region.
Figure 2.
Wigber Low cemetery, c. AD 625–685: a) & b) plan and photograph of burial 4 (WIG 03) with sword (copyright University of Sheffield; plan redrawn from Collis
Reference Collis
1983 by A. Bloxam); c) crystal ball amulet (diameter 36mm), burial 9 (WIG 06); d) gold and beaver-tooth pendant (length 37mm) found close to burial 9 (copyright Sheffield Museums Trust).
By the mid-eleventh century, the Domesday survey (Db) (undertaken to record the use and taxable value of land across Norman England) suggests that large-scale lead production occurred in the Peak District during the reign of Edward the Confessor (1042–1066). Mines/smelting centres (plu(m)baria) were recorded at royal manors in the Low Peak, at Matlock (one mine), Wirksworth (three mines), Bakewell (one mine) and Ashford (one mine) (Db (Domesday Book), F. (Folio) 272b–d; Morgan
Reference Morgan
1978). The manors of Ashford, Bakewell and Hope each owed annually five ‘cart-loads’ of lead (with one cart-load equalling approximately 2100lbs) in Geld-tax in 1066, with 50 sheets of lead per cart-load (Db, F. 272d-273a; Morgan
Reference Morgan
1978). In 1086, the manors of Darley, Matlock, Wirksworth, Ashbourne and Parwich owed annually 40 pounds in ‘pure silver’ (argenti puri) in Geld, the only use of this specific term in Domesday Book (Db, F. 272c; Morgan
Reference Morgan
1978), possibly reflecting some extraction of the small amounts of silver in galena-lead ore. These silver payments were made at the start of the European ‘silver shortage’ of c. 1050–1150 (Spufford
Reference Spufford
1988: 95–99). However, use of British silver is difficult to identify in a recent, small-scale lead-isotope analysis of twelfth-century British coinage (Savage et al.
Reference Savage
2024).
A castle was constructed by William Peverel (Peveril Castle) in the High Peak before 1086, at the berewick (linked secondary settlement) of the royal estate centre at Hope, called Pechesers, likely named after a lead mine adjacent to the castle (Db, F. 276b; Morgan
Reference Morgan
1978; Figure 1b). The settlement around the mine and castle later became known as Castleton and was the administrative centre and key focus of lead mining in the medieval High Peak region (Loveluck et al.
Reference Loveluck
2020: OSM 5: 39). Excavations from 2009–2026 (currently unpublished) led jointly by the University of Sheffield and Castleton Historical Society have uncovered unfurnished graves within Castleton at two locations: Joule Yard, dating between the seventh and eleventh centuries AD; and Spital Field, on the eastern outskirts of the village associated with a medieval hospital building, dating from the twelfth–late fifteenth centuries AD (Figure 3). Individuals from these Castleton cemeteries provide the principal Peak District population sample in this study.
Figure 3.
The Castleton cemeteries: a) Joule Yard; b) Spital Field (figure by C. Merrony & A. Darlington).
The date range of the cemetery populations also covers a period when more comprehensive documentary evidence for the scale of Peak District lead production is available. For example, the Pipe Rolls (recording taxation owed and paid to the royal Treasury) show that Peak District lead production reached its medieval zenith from c. 1180–1215 (Loveluck et al.
Reference Loveluck
2020: 476, OSM5: 37–52). A decline in production followed, with renewed cycles of ‘boom and bust’ from the late thirteenth–fifteenth centuries (Blanchard
Reference Blanchard
2005: 1400). An ice-core drilled from the north-west-facing slope at Colle Gnifetti (Swiss-Italian Alps) reveals lead-pollution trends identical to Peak District production cycles, with high points from c. 1180–1215 and decline in the mid-thirteenth century (More et al.
Reference More
2017: 213; Loveluck et al.
Reference Loveluck
2020: 476). Here, we investigate levels of lead pollution within a Peak District population against these historical production and environmental pollution records.
Methodological approach
This study has the following objectives:
1) to provide radiocarbon dates for the establishment and changing scales of lead production in the medieval Peak District;
2) to use lead contaminant concentrations in the teeth of a regional population sample to establish involvement in lead production by comparison with period-based societal norms;
3) to assess any evidence of population movement into the region, possibly linked to mining;
4) to analyse evidence for differentiation by social rank, role, gender and age from lead pollution levels among the population sample; and
5) to begin to evaluate the impact of lead pollution on human health and the environment in this period.
The population sample
The early- to late-medieval population sample analysed here focuses primarily on Castleton (53°20′35.52″N, 1°46′31.08″W). Initial radiocarbon dating of unfurnished inhumation graves at Joule Yard showed that people had been buried in this location, presumably associated with a settlement, since the seventh–eighth centuries AD; when it may already have been linked to the estate centre at Hope. Graves associated with the medieval hospital in Spital Field provide radiocarbon determinations that post-date the Norman Conquest (AD 1066), when Castleton became the administrative centre of the High Peak. To identify whether any of the individuals had been exposed to lead production during childhood, a sample of 10 individuals was selected on the basis of tooth-enamel preservation, with five each coming from the Joule Yard and Spital Field cemeteries. All sampled individuals were radiocarbon dated (Figure 4). The individuals from Joule Yard have date ranges that cluster from the early seventh–early eleventh centuries, while those from Spital Field cluster from the mid-eleventh–early sixteenth centuries. The teeth of two later Iron Age (c. 400 BC–AD 43) individuals from the nearby site of Eldon Hole were also sampled to provide a pre-large-scale mining comparison for lead levels (online supplementary material (OSM) 1). No sufficiently preserved teeth from the Romano–British period (c. AD 43–400) were available for analysis due to the tradition of disarticulated burial, often in caves (Brownlee & Klevnäs
Reference Brownlee and Klevnäs
2024: 1617).
Figure 4.
Radiocarbon dates from the population sample (figure by A. Bloxam).
To obtain regional comparative data, we also selected teeth from five inhumation graves at Wigber Low (Figure 1b). Four graves, found in 1975–76 (Chesterman
Reference Chesterman and Collis
1983; Collis
Reference Collis
1983), were dated through artefact seriations of ‘Anglo-Saxon’ grave-goods, linked to over 100 radiocarbon dates: two females from phase ASF-E, AD 625–685 and two males from phases ASM-D to F, AD 565–685 (Bayliss et al.
Reference Bayliss
2013: 485). One of the males (Burial 4 south, sample WIG 03, Figure 2a) was buried with a mid-late sixth-century sword, probably an heirloom, when interred in the seventh century (Ager
Reference Ager and Collis
1983: 77). A new radiocarbon date obtained from burial 9 (WIG-06), a female buried with a crystal ball amulet, iron-bound wooden box and knife (Figure 2b; Foster & Collis
Reference Foster and Collis
1988: 235–37), produced a date of AD 610–665 (Figure 4), indicating that the seriation dating is generally reliable. The only unfurnished grave sampled from the otherwise seventh-century furnished cemetery at Wigber Low (male burial 7; sample WIG-05) was assigned a date range of AD 625–685, using the more reliable female seriation.
Analytical methods
Assessment of the extent to which the population sample was involved in lead production or exposed to environmental lead pollution was achieved through measurement of lead concentrations in the dental enamel. A sample of enamel was taken from each individual, from a second molar, premolar or third molar (OSM1). Enamel does not remodel after its initial formation, so these samples provide a closed record of lead concentrations during childhood, between the ages of approximately four and 12 years. Excavated evidence from the seventh–tenth-century lead-silver mines and processing zones in Melle, western France, suggests that children could have been contaminated while washing and dressing ore before these were smelted, or as bystanders to these activities (Téreygeol
Reference Téreygeol
1999: 23–25).
The enamel samples were prepared and analysed using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry at the British Geological Survey (BGS) (see OSM2). The resulting lead concentrations were then compared across the regional population sample, against median averages for lead concentration from Neolithic to post-medieval population data across Britain (Montgomery et al.
Reference Montgomery
2010: tab. 11.4; Millard et al.
Reference Millard and Zuckermann
2014; Moore et al.
Reference Moore
2021: fig. 1; see OSM2) and with a sixteenth-century silver- and lead-mining population from Sala, Sweden (Price et al.
Reference Price
2017).
To address the extent to which the sampled Peak District individuals were native to the region, we analysed strontium (Sr), oxygen (O) and lead (Pb) isotopes in the enamel (see OSM1 & OSM2).

title: This is a story of a Figma bug – Aresluna
content:
Marcin Wichary
20 May 2021 / 28 tweets / 19 photos
This is a story of a Figma bug that wasn’t a bug at all
This is an archive of a Twitter thread from 2021. On that day, Figma allowed various people working there to do a “takeover” of their social account, and I was one of these people.
This is a story of a Figma bug that wasn’t a bug at all.

In November of 2019, one of our users reported this:
3.9K / 1.7K / 20 May 2021 / 1:25pm
In short, pressing Shift+2 using one key worked, but pressing Shift+2 using the numeric keypad key didn’t.

Curiously, the bug only happened on Windows, and not on a Mac.
121 / 4 / 20 May 2021 / 1:26pm
Turns out this bug goes back all the way to… 1977.

This was the time when IBM, the #1 computer maker of that time, continued their attempts to conquer the burgeoning small, personal computer market. (Before, most of their computers looked like the one below.)
201 / 17 / 20 May 2021 / 1:27pm
In 1977, they released IBM System/34 – a “small computer” for small businesses – with a keyboard and display called 5251.
107 / 20 May 2021 / 1:28pm
System/34 was still be a pretty pricey machine, costing 5 or 6 figures. Part of that hefty price was a beautiful beam spring keyboard – with the numeric keypad on the right, but arrow keys on the very left. (Arrow keys were not as important in computers around then.)
107 / 1 / 20 May 2021 / 1:29pm
Then, in 1980, IBM released another computer, called System/23, or Datamaster. This one you could lift and carry, although you should still be careful (it was almost 100 lbs!). It was also much cheaper, coming in at $9,000.
102 / 2 / 20 May 2021 / 1:30pm
The machine looked like this. The company reused pretty much the layout of the IBM 5251 keyboard… although it came sporting a new design language, and then-brand-new buckling spring switches.
94 / 1 / 20 May 2021 / 1:32pm
As far as I know, the machine wasn’t a huge success. But the one that followed, IBM 5150 from 1981, was. You might have heard it by its more common name: IBM PC.
113 / 5 / 20 May 2021 / 1:33pm
IBM PC was a pretty fast project, so the designers decided to just grab the keyboard from the Datamaster verbatim, and just change the functions of some keys. The left block was replaced by function keys, and the arrow keys were moved to the right.
103 / 1 / 20 May 2021 / 1:34pm
The arrow keys were more important then than in 1977, to navigate spreadsheets (also brand new!) and menus. But the limitations of the 5251 layout meant they had to share space with the numeric keypad.
89 / 1 / 20 May 2021 / 1:35pm
And so the engineers created a key that could toggle between the arrows and the numeric keypad. They called it Num Lock.
132 / 3 / 20 May 2021 / 1:35pm
But this wasn’t great. Imagine using a spreadsheet for a while. You type in the number, then you want to move to another cell with arrows, then type another number. Pressing Num Lock over and over again to switch between the modes would be slow, infuriating, and flow-reducing…
97 / 1 / 20 May 2021 / 1:36pm
…particularly since Num Lock didn’t even have a light.

(Imagine needing to press Caps Lock every time you wanted to capitalize a letter at the beginning of a sentence, and then needing to press it again, never seeing its current state!)
117 / 6 / 20 May 2021 / 1:36pm
So the engineers came up with a power-user shortcut… and since the Shift was a natural counterpart in the Caps Lock world, it could also do the same here!

The solution: you could hold Shift and press the arrow/numeric key to quickly reverse its current mode.
142 / 4 / 20 May 2021 / 1:37pm
This was ingenious. Your other hand was free, after all, and holding Shift like this – some people call it a spring-loaded mode, or a “quasimode” (RIP Jef Raskin) – is much faster. You could type your number, press Shift+2 to go down to the next cell, and continue calculations.
145 / 20 May 2021 / 1:37pm
…aaaaand at this point you should already know what was happening with the Figma bug.

Although there’s one more delightful ingredient:
162 / 20 May 2021 / 1:38pm
In the late 1980s IBM finally switched the keyboard layout in response to people complaining about a bunch of issues with the 5150 keyboard. What happened was what many consider the “God’s keyboard“ – IBM Model M, with an extended 100-ish-key layout that is still with us today.
164 / 7 / 20 May 2021 / 1:38pm
That layout had its arrow keys separate from the numeric keypad… but since 5 years has passed, some people already got used to the Num Lock situation, so that had to be preserved also. You don’t mess up with people’s motor memory!
123 / 2 / 20 May 2021 / 1:39pm
And if you have to keep Num Lock, you also have to keep the Shift shortcut… and that‘s exactly what was happening to the user that reported the Shift+2 bug, almost 40 years after the decisions were made.
187 / 9 / 20 May 2021 / 1:39pm
The shortcut from MS-DOS was preserved in code through all the versions of Windows, from 1.0 all the way to 10!
174 / 5 / 20 May 2021 / 1:39pm
And so, in Figma, Shift+2 on the regular keyboard worked as “Zoom to selection,” but pressing Shift+2 on the numeric keypad was interpreted as “↓” – and obviously did something different.
148 / 20 May 2021 / 1:40pm
This also explains why this was never an issue on a Mac! Infamously, the first Mac had neither arrow keys (to force programmers to make mouse-oriented software) nor a numeric keyboard.
200 / 2 / 20 May 2021 / 1:40pm
By the time they were added in 1987, they were both separate keys in sections, so the Num Lock never had to happen.
131 / 3 / 20 May 2021 / 1:40pm
Fortunately, at that point, browsers gave us enough information to disambiguate between the one Shift+2 and the other Shift+2… so we could fix the bug and close it.

Even though you could argue it was never a bug – just an older, barely documented convention.
203 / 20 May 2021 / 1:41pm
And how did I learn this lesson? In the research for a book on the history of keyboards I’m working on, I talked to Dave Bradley who was the engineer behind those decisions back in 1981!
David Bradley (engineer)
wikipedia.org
369 / 6 / 20 May 2021 / 1:41pm
Fun fact: He’s also a person behind Ctrl+Alt+Del… but that’s a whole different story.
306 / 7 / 20 May 2021 / 1:41pm
(By the way, if you like that kind of stuff, here are two more stories for you:

1. It seems like every place I end up working, I deal with a bug like this:
The curious case of the disappearing Polish S
medium.com
229 / 27 / 20 May 2021 / 3:30pm
2. And this is a story of a first bug I had to fix, long time ago… a software fix to a hardware problem, just to play a game I really wanted to play:
A hacker’s guide to bending the universe
aresluna.org
203 / 13 / 20 May 2021 / 3:31pm

title: The Importance of Limitations for Creativity and Learning - ratfactor
content:
This is a card in Dave's Virtual Box of Cards.
The Importance of Limitations for Creativity and Learning
Page created: 2023-09-20
Updated: 2025-10-06
creativity, learning
The other day, my kids started messing around (at home) with an online document writing platform their school uses. They’d discovered a fun little easter egg. I watched them laugh and play with the feature - pushing its limits and ultimately crashing the browser.
These same kids have messed about in Scratch (wikipedia.org) through the school as well, but they rarely stick with it for very long.
I think Scratch is brilliantly done and I don’t wish to speak ill of it.
But it struck me how the limitations of the easter egg made it more compelling to play with. The feature was a little buggy and did not handle multiple instances very well. This led to interesting behavior as they added more and more instances to the page.
This "toy" had way less features than Scratch, but it was pretty free-form in use and it was easy to invoke. It also had severe limitations and was easy to break.
I think Scratch is so featureful that it is intimidating to newcomers. The paradox of having so many toys is that it’s hard to know which one to play with.
In both learning and creativity, I think there’s a lot to be said for a very simple toolbox that invites play but doesn’t present too many options at first.
I think a lot of people can relate to this in the visual arts: Give me a nice set of paints and brushes and a big blank canvas and watch me agonize about what to paint. But put a ragged piece of scrap paper and a pencil in front of me and watch me start to doodle!
Are these the same principles at work? It feels like they might be.
See also: free-verse-programming
Why other people’s dreams are boring
Another type of limitation is the structure of a story. That structure could be anything, but it might be that the story is told in 3-acts or that it is entirely based on the motivations of the characters, or something else. It doesn’t have to be much of a limit, but it’s something.
I think the lack of limits in the form of structure is what makes people’s dreams (generally) so boring to hear about - there’s no limits and no structure and no rules. It’s just seemingly-random events.
A movie that breaks its own internal rules is frustrating, but dreams don’t even have rules to break, so it’s not even interesting to criticize them!
Small budgets
A big-budget movie can be clever and amazing. But I think that requires the style and restraint of the director. Otherwise, you can just make the first thing that comes to your mind - which is probably going to be the most obvious thing to come to your (and your audience’s) mind!
But a small-budget movie has to be clever to be any good at all. If you’ve got $300 for props, you’re going to have to come up with something different…and that can lead to surprise and delight because you did something unexpected with the material available.
Again, big budget stuff can be surprising and delightful, too, but I think that requires a ton of willful determination on the part of the artists involved. That’s might be why the successful ones can be pretty forceful personalities. (Not that I think artistic genius and being a nasty person need to go hand-in-hand either. I’m not promoting that idea here. I don’t think that’s the same thing.)

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will face challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a presidential election runoff on October 25 [File: Evaristo Sa/AFP]
By AP and Reuters
Published On 16 Oct 2026
16 Oct 2026
Employees at Meta have acknowledged in internal communications that the Instagram accounts of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were negatively affected by restrictions during the country’s election, media reports say.
The messages, reported on Friday by Brazilian daily Folha de S Paulo, also acknowledged the platform recommended the profile of Lula challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as well as his WhatsApp channel. Folha, the Sao Paulo-based paper, cited messages it had reviewed.

end of list
Meta told the Reuters news agency that the technical issues cited in the report were already public and the conversations it referenced related solely to the severity of the issues, not political interference.
“Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it added in a statement.
Lula, the left-wing incumbent, will face right-wing challenger Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff on October 25, following a stronger-than-expected performance by the senator in the first-round vote earlier this month.
Friday’s report came on the heels of a Brazilian court ruling on Thursday that ordered Meta to immediately adopt measures to provide equal treatment of the two candidates ahead of the runoff.
The ruling by a judge in Brazil’s top electoral court was made shortly after Lula filed a complaint that accused the tech giant – which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp – of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election.
Justice Marco Aurelio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies.
Advertisement
Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,700) per day if it fails to comply.
According to Lula’s party, some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach. Options for reactions, sharing, audio or accelerated speed were also missing.

title: Node2Shell Brotli vuln (CVE-2026-111497) evolves to HTTP2Shell, as libraries and apps using HTTP are affected.
content:
Blog
Vulnerabilities & Threats
Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell. Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497) blast radius affects many libraries & apps using HTTPs.
Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell. Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497) blast radius affects many libraries & apps using HTTPs.
Buckle up.
Written by
Dania Durnas
Published on:
Oct 23, 2026
Last updated on:
Oct 24, 2026
TL;DR
⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well.

On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available.

Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available.

Update 4:12PM PT: Patches are available for libbrotli, Python, C++, NodeJS, bun, Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default.
Update 4:15 PM PT: OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here.
‍
What is Brotli?
Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
What is CVE-2026-111497?
CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.
A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.
OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses.
The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update. 
‍You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet.
‍You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel. 
Python
C++
Libbrotil
NodeJS
As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli
How to patch HTTP2Shell CVE-2026-111497
For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:
Node.js: upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line.
Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to 1.2.1 or later. For older release lines, use patched 1.0.10 or 1.1.1.
Python packages: upgrade Brotli to 1.2.1 or later and brotlicffi to 1.2.1.0 or later, wherever installed.
curl / libcurl: update its Brotli dependency to 1.2.1, a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build.
Bun: upgrade to 1.4.4 or later. Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun.
Envoy: upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8, or a newer release in a supported branch. 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported.
Istio: the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2. Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life.
Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number.
Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider.
Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.
‍
Fixed releases, reviewed October 23, 2026
Project Patch status Fixed versions Notes
Node.js Patch available 22.23.4 · 24.22.1 · 26.12.1 Use a supported release line.
Bun Patch available 1.4.4 Includes Brotli 1.2.1.
Envoy Patch available 1.40.0 · 1.39.3 · 1.38.6 · 1.37.8 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but 1.36 is unsupported. Use a supported branch.
Istio Patch available 1.29.9 · 1.30.6 · 1.31.2 1.29 is end of life, so move to a supported line.
Google Brotli (upstream) Patch available 1.0.10 · 1.1.1 · 1.2.1 Choose the fixed release for your library branch.
What to do if you can't upgrade yet
These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade:
Python applications: where Brotli support is optional, uninstall both Brotli and brotlicffi from affected environments. Remove dependency extras such as httpx[brotli] and any other requirements that would reinstall them, then regenerate dependency locks and rebuild/restart workloads. HTTPX, Requests, and urllib3 retain gzip and deflate support without these optional packages. However, a server that sends Brotli anyway may produce an unreadable response or an application error; automatic fallback is not guaranteed.
Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products.
Incoming HTTP requests: reject requests whose Content-Encoding includes br at the reverse proxy, load balancer, or application middleware, before any vulnerable decoder processes the body. Match br case-insensitively, including within lists of encodings. 
Outbound HTTP requests: remove br from Accept-Encoding. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late.
Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header.
Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths.
How Aikido helps with CVE-2026-111497
Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images, and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies. Your dashboard shows which services still run a vulnerable version, so you can upgrade the ones that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies first. 
Once you've upgraded, Aikido checks if the finding is gone.
The timeline
Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 22nd NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. Users were exposed if their app or a library decompresses bad Brotli data (e.g. the built-in fetch(), body-parser).
The next day, Python released a security update that patches the same flaw; Python packages were also vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497. Brotli flaw may affect even more languages and service applications, given how widely integrated the library is downstream. It turns out OpenAI had found this back in February.
Techincal details of CVE-2026-111497
The flaw sits in DecodeBlockTypeAndLength(), which handles block switches, the points where a Brotli stream changes which Huffman tree it uses. In vulnerable versions the function returns a plain boolean, and BROTLI_FALSE can mean either "this stream is malformed" or "I need more input." Callers can't tell the two apart, and on the fast path the decoder discards the return value entirely.
A crafted stream can declare a single block type and then exhaust that block's length, which forces a switch that can't succeed. The decoder then either reports that it needs more input for a stream that's complete, or keeps decoding with the block state it already had. That second path leads to the out-of-bounds write.
The upstream fix, google/brotli commit 0ed4268, makes the function return an error code and adds a new error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (-17). Decoding now stops on a format error on both the safe and fast paths. OSM diffed the Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 source distributions and found that 1.2.1 differs only in the version bump and the decoder changes from that commit.
‍
‍
Brotli vulnerabilities in Python libraries (CVE-2026-111497)
The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497)  affects Python. Two PyPI packages, Brotli and brotlicffi, compile the same vulnerable Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles. An official advisory was posted on GitHub. Brotli has 82.8 million downloads per month.
You're affected if any Python environment you run has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier, or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x, installed. Popular HTTP clients such as requests and httpx load these packages automatically when they're present. Some packages automatically install Brotli as a dependency such as Scrapy, while others require explicit mention of it. An attacker can reach the vulnerable decoder by sending a malicious Brotli response to a request your app makes, or by sending your app a request body compressed with Brotli. That means an app can be exposed without importing Brotli anywhere in its own code. It’s a popular transitive dependency, so check your systems.
To fix it, upgrade to the patched releases:
Brotli -> 1.2.1
brotlicffi -> 1.2.1.0
The release notes for both fixed versions don't mention the CVE. As of October 23, advisory databases don't map it to either PyPI package yet, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won't flag these versions.
Who is affected by CVE-2026-111497 in Python?
You’re affected if any of your Python environments have one of these packages installed:
Package Affected versions Fixed version
Brotli (PyPI) 1.2.0 and earlier 1.2.1
brotlicffi (PyPI) 1.2.0.x 1.2.1.0
Your code doesn’t have to import either package. These HTTP clients advertise Accept-Encoding: br and decode Brotli responses automatically:
urllib3 (and therefore requests) when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed
httpx with the brotli extra
aiohttp when Brotli is installed
Scrapy, and anything built on the clients above
Attacker data can reach the decoder through two routes:
Outbound requests. Your app fetches a Brotli response from a server an attacker controls, such as through a webhook delivery, URL preview, crawler or “fetch this URL” feature.
Inbound requests. Your framework or middleware decodes a request body sent with Content-Encoding: br, which is the Python equivalent of the Express 5 case in Node.js.
How to fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python
The fix is a package upgrade, and it takes four steps:
Upgrade whichever package you have installed with pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" or pip install -U "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0". If you use a lockfile with Poetry, uv, or pip-tools, update the constraint and regenerate the lockfile.
Rebuild your container images and any wheels that bundle either package. An image built on a vulnerable version stays vulnerable until you rebuild it.
Check every environment you run, including laptops, CI runners, servers and containers. Many projects pull in Brotli through an HTTP client extra, so look at your full resolved dependency tree.
Rely on a manual check for now. pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety won't report this until the advisory databases map the CVE to the PyPI packages.
If your Python Brotli bindings came from a Linux distribution package instead of PyPI, the fix comes through your distribution, so check its security advisory as well.
What is the Python Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)?
Python Brotli vulnerability refers to CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder flaw known as Node2Shell, as it affects Python packages on PyPI. The CVE record pairs CWE-252 (unchecked return value) with CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).
How serious is CVE-2026-111497 for Python, and is it being exploited?
The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and Node.js rates it high severity. OSM built Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 with AddressSanitizer and ran a crafted stream through both. Version 1.2.0 consumed all of the roughly 23 MB stream and kept reporting that it needed more input, whether the stream arrived in one piece or in chunks as small as one byte. Version 1.2.1 rejected the stream with error -17 every time.
OSM didn't pursue memory corruption or code execution in the Python extension. The decoder code is the same code that researchers exploited against an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build, as Imperva and others reported. For Node.js, The Hacker News reported no exploitation in the wild as of October 22.
Treat it as urgent anyway. The bug is a memory-safety flaw in a component that handles untrusted network input, and the fix is a routine version bump. Services that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies should go first.
How to check if your Python app is exposed
Check installed versions with pip show Brotli brotlicffi in each environment, and with docker run --rm <image> pip show Brotli brotlicffi for each container image.
Find what pulls the packages in. Run pipdeptree -r -p Brotli to see which dependencies require it, and search your lockfiles with grep -i brotli poet

title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions - EPFL
content:
Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions
LogSync chips, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0
EPFL researchers have developed an implantable neural chip that tracks communication across brain regions, identifying cognitive and emotional states in real time.
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. Even among closed-loop, or adaptive systems, many rely on signals recorded from a single brain region. This is a major limitation for psychiatric disorders, where clinically relevant information may be distributed across networks of interacting brain regions.
“Our work is based on the growing body of research suggesting that psychiatric disorders arise more from disruptions in communication between brain regions than from dysfunction of any single region,” explains Mahsa Shoaran, head of the Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab in EPFL’s School of Engineering and Neuro-X Institute.
The INL team at EPFL's Geneva campus. From left: Amitabh Yadav, Jieun Joo, Mahsa Shoaran, Jinhan Liu, and Daney Alex. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0
Shoaran and her team have developed a low-power, implantable neural system-on-chip. Dubbed LogSync, it records brain activity and extracts biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves (oscillations) and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. A machine-learning algorithm then analyzes these network-level biomarkers to distinguish cognitive and emotional states, and generate stimulation triggers when specific states are detected.
The work, published in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, was developed as part of a CHF 6.6 million grant from the US National Institute for Mental health (NIMH) to develop implantable systems capable of measuring and controlling oscillatory brain networks for severe psychiatric illnesses, particularly mood and anxiety disorders. It builds on the lab's previous work on brain-to-text decoding and closed-loop neuromodulation, extending these concepts to network-level biomarkers and adaptive decoding for future psychiatric therapies.
More targeted stimulation at lower power
The researchers evaluated LogSync using human brain recordings from previous psychiatric experiments. One dataset captured changes in cognitive engagement while performing a mental task, while another captured emotional arousal as participants viewed video clips. The algorithm distinguished these cognitive and emotional states from the neural recordings alone. In further experiments conducted in rats at the University of Minnesota, the implant tracked ongoing oscillations and generated stimulation triggers at predefined phases of brain activity.
The LogSync chip, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 CC-BY-SA 4.0
Shoaran says that major challenge was achieving all this functionality while working within the very limited power budget of an implantable system.
“Our entire system is co-designed, meaning the algorithms and hardware are developed together with the constraints of implant in mind. This approach helped us achieve network-level neural signal processing and decoding on a single chip, while keeping power consumption under 200 microwatts — a fraction of that typically required by many implantable neural-interface systems,” she says. Another innovation is LogSync’s use of logarithmic computations, which simplify the complex operations needed for brain-network analysis and real-time biomarker extraction and decoding.
LogSync's initial validation focused on psychiatric applications. But the capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation is broadly applicable across next-generation neurotechnology, including adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and emerging focused-ultrasound interfaces.
In parallel, the laboratory is developing new machine-learning methods that learn directly from neural recordings rather than predefined biomarkers. Their recent ICML 2026 work, which uses self-supervised learning to capture neural activity across regions, channels, and time, supports broader efforts to bring intelligent neural interfaces closer to clinical applications, including through Infera Neuro, an EPFL spin-off co-founded by Shoaran.

title: Reactive Optimizers

← Xingjian Bai
Reactive Optimizers
Xingjian Bai, Jia-Hao Liang, Jayden Teoh, Vincent Sitzmann
October 2026
TL;DR We put an agent at the heart of the optimizer. It watches the training dynamics, reacts to them, and rewrites the optimizer’s source code as training goes. When no recipe has been tuned for a task, it matches or beats the best recipe one could pick off the shelf, across image and language tasks. Further, we demonstrate that it spontaneously comes up with sophisticated schedules and intricate strategies to prevent loss spikes and escape overfitting. Try it on your own training run with the OPAL package.

Today, the recipe used to optimize a deep neural network is typically completely determined before training even begins. A great deal of human ingenuity has gone into priors regarding how training should progress: adaptive step sizes [1], preconditioning [2, 3], orthogonalized updates [4, 5], schedules tied to the training step [6, 7], and learning rates scaled with model size [8]. Automated discovery [9, 10, 11, 12] searches across many runs for better optimizers. Whether hand-crafted or automatically discovered, the optimizer then runs unchanged through the end of training, adapting, if at all, according to rules written in advance. This scope leaves the following questions unanswered: How should an optimizer respond to an unexpected loss spike or stall? What if one module’s gradients start to oscillate while the others keep improving smoothly? And when a new type of architecture trains poorly with Adam or Muon, is the architecture worse, or has it not yet met an optimizer suited to it?
In this post, we attempt to expand the scope of conventional optimizers and make them reactive to the training itself, leading to an ever-adapting optimizer inside a single training run. This reactive optimizer reasons on the spot and writes the weight update rule for each parameter group. Directly writing optimization code, it has the freedom to implement complicated schedules, respond to training accidents, and customize the optimizer for the single training episode in which it exists. Building on earlier attempts to adapt optimizers during training [12, 13, 14] and to let a model direct its own fine-tuning [15], the reactive optimizer is entirely zero-shot, with nothing learned or retained from repeated runs, and puts the optimizer’s entire algorithm up for rewriting.
We start with a practical situation, with tasks from image generation and language modeling, in which a reactive optimizer can do much better than static ones. We then turn to the emergent properties of the reactive optimizer, including sophisticated scheduling, suppressing loss spikes, and escaping overfitting. Lastly, we ask what all this costs and how practical it is at scale. We expect the reactive optimizer to grow only stronger with each generation of agents, to be most useful exactly where no recipe exists yet (for a new architecture or a new dataset), and to be one step toward solving the puzzles of deep learning optimization.
Contents
1. Training without a recipe
2. Updating with spontaneous analysis
3. What is dynamically changing during optimization?
4. Real-world applicability
5. Conclusion
1. Training without a recipe
Suppose a PhD student has a new idea: a model of their own design, or a new dataset on which to train a transformer. They have one GPU for a single day only and a modest allotment of LLM API tokens, allowing for just one serious training run. What should the student do? The obvious course of action would be to pick the most standard training recipe, or one from a recent paper, and cope with the possibility that it might be unsuitable for their scenario, with spiking/stalling loss, etc.
The underlying question is broader: when bounded by GPU time, researcher time, or wall-clock time, how can a deep learning model be trained to its best performance without knowing the optimal optimization recipe in advance? New architectures, modalities, languages, and scientific data all fall into this setting, where few people can afford a sweep at scale.
A reactive optimizer offers another way to use that budget: it spends LLM tokens in place of GPU/human hours. With optimizers reacting to training incidents and adjusting themselves, much of the burden of recipe tuning can be reduced.
Results in brief
We start from the optimization track (Track 3) of modded-nanogpt [16], a language-model pre-training task (training a 162M GPT on FineWeb) with many recipes tuned specifically for this one setting. From this task, we create two slightly differing natural settings: (1) the same model trained on an alternate language dataset (we select Chinese, Thai, and Kyrgyz), and (2) the original setup with a quarter of the batch size. Neither comes with a recipe tuned for that setting, so we compare the reactive optimizer with the natural options one would have if they wanted to one-shot the new training: adopting five leaderboard recipes with natural adjustments. In all these new settings, the reactive optimizer outperforms or matches the best baseline (Figure 1).
We also apply the reactive optimizer directly to Goldfish [17], which proposes a dataset of 350 languages and trains one small GPT per dataset with a standard recipe not tuned for each language. This makes it an ideal ground to test the optimizer’s adaptiveness in one shot. On the Amharic dataset, the official recipe ends at 83.48 bits per sentence on held-out FLORES-200 text (lower is better); the reactive optimizer, initialized with this same recipe, ends at 81.11 in one shot (on Swahili, we obtain a similar gain). Sweeping the learning rate of the standard recipe finds a static recipe that ends ahead of the reactive optimizer, at 80.89, but the reactive optimizer initialized from that swept recipe ends ahead again, at 80.73.
We also try the reactive optimizer on image generation, a direction where the literature usually does not sweep optimization hyperparameters, since diffusion-model design and optimizer design are viewed as mostly orthogonal1
1 For example, the standard recipes of DiT and SiT [19] train with AdamW at one constant learning rate. That has begun to change, with Muon and its variants taken up for diffusion transformers (CMuon [20]; Li et al. [21]; RAEv2’s GMuon [22]) and a recent controlled benchmark of optimizers for diffusion models [23].
. It ends ahead of the official recipe on LightningDiT-XL/1 ([18]; FID-50K 1.83 against 2.18 with guidance, 4.33 against 5.15 without), whose official recipe trains with AdamW, and on RAEv2-B (3.19 against 3.39), whose recipe trains with a Muon variant.
Figure 1 shows these runs, each with Claude Opus 5.5 powering the agent; we name our reactive optimizer OPAL (OPtimizer with an Agent in the Loop). Together, these results show that in one-shot settings, a reactive optimizer can lead to a better solution than adhering to a predetermined recipe.

In modded-nanogpt, #2 is AdamW, #21 is Shampoo, #36 is a tuned Muon, and #30 and #46 are more elaborate Muon-based recipes.
Beyond the practical benefit, we are intrigued by the spontaneous decisions made by the zero-shot agent, after observing and analyzing the training dynamics in its own way. In the next two sections, we explore what the reactive optimizer chooses to watch and what it changes in response.
2. Updating with spontaneous analysis

Figure 2. The two programs the agent writes and rewrites iteratively during training. With code as the entire interface, we give the agent maximal freedom to choose what to watch and what to change.
Figure 2 shows how an agent updates the optimizer code on the fly. Concretely, we allow the agent to rewrite a file, updater.py, used in every step of optimization. We use code as the entire interface since this allows the agent to easily alter any part of the optimization. Yet, before the agent can make changes, it must observe, on its own, how training is progressing, leading to the second program it can rewrite, analysis.py.
What information should the agent use to make its decisions? Raw training states would be impractical: the weights, activations, and gradients would swamp its context. Instead, the statistics and geometry of training dynamics could be helpful for decisions, such as the gradient norm of each parameter group, the size of an update next to the weights it changes, the cosine between consecutive gradients, and which tensors exhibit unusually large gradient spikes. Therefore, as with the optimizer, we give the agent the most freedom: it writes a program, analysis.py, to extract whatever it wants to know from the training dynamics. Its self-written probes run throughout training, taking from the state of training whatever the agent asks for and handing it to the agent for its next decision.
We complete the bidirectional loop. Through analysis.py, training reaches the agent in whatever form the agent chooses to see it, and through updater.py, the agent’s decisions reach every step of training. The two programs let the agent devise new optimization algorithms along the way with maximum flexibility.
3. What is dynamically changing during optimization?
In this section, we look at what the reactive optimizer does throughout training, examining the decisions behind these results. As a summary, Figure 3 shows when, how, and why each agent edits its code.
