So while we didn't outperform the champ on average, a median slowdown percentage in the single digits compared to such a carefully-tuned SIMD-powered C library is wild. It's frankly not a result I knew was achievable going in, since Roc is a functional language with automatic memory management racing against code that doesn't have to do bounds checks. (Bounds checks have a cost, but then again, the last time a skipped bounds check in C compression code led to a major Remote Code Execution vulnerability was yesterday.)
The graph shows more detail than just the median gap. On the worst-case inputs, roc-deflate was 18% slower than libdeflate, but on the best-case inputs, roc-deflate was slightly over 18% faster! That's not because Roc has some magical optimization that C can't access; it's just that the two implementations are different, and although on average roc-deflate is slower, for certain inputs it happens to be faster. So while it's possible to get a speedup by switching from libdeflate to roc-deflate, you shouldn't expect it on average.
To be clear, C's performance ceiling is higher than Roc's. For any input where roc-deflate currently outperforms libdeflate, C code can close that gap. The reverse is not true; Roc code is memory-safe, does automatic reference counting, checks bounds, and supports no Rust-style unsafe to opt out of any of that. These properties give Roc code stronger safety guarantees than code written in C, Zig, Rust, and other languages that allow full access to the hardware—and the price it pays for those guarantees is a lower performance ceiling.
Obviously we can't extrapolate from this one result about how close Roc can get to C in the general case, but now something has been demonstrated that nobody knew was achievable before. As far as I know, this is the most optimization effort that has been put into any Roc package to date, so how close others can get to this result is a complete unknown right now. So while I'm thrilled by this result, I'm fully aware that we won't know how well it generalizes until we've optimized a wider sample of real-world Roc code bases!
What the Performance Gap Buys
An obvious question is "Why settle for any amount slower?" If you could get C levels of performance, why not use libdeflate itself and close that remaining gap?
A pure-Roc implementation has several advantages over a pure-C one:
Memory safety. Roc code is fully memory-safe and has no language primitives that let you opt out of it. This code is only able to approach C levels of performance because Roc's optimization pipeline determined that many bounds checks and reference counting operations were provably safe to optimize away. Compression packages written in pure Roc don't have access to the unchecked memory operation that caused yesterday's Brotli Remote Code Execution vulnerability.
No side effects. Roc's type system infers which functions are pure and which can perform side effects. Pure functions' types use a thin arrow, like Bool -> Bool, whereas effectful functions use a thick arrow, like Bool => Bool. (As with memory safety, Roc enforces this and supports no way to opt out.) So when you see that roc-deflate's functions have only thin arrows in their annotations, you know they really are pure functions.
Supply-Chain Security. Roc does not have an arbitrary FFI, meaning you know for sure that roc-deflate's pure functions can't even attempt to do I/O or access arbitrary memory. Given the explosion in supply chain attacks, it's valuable to know that the damage a malicious actor can do with a pure function in a compromised Roc package is limited to returning the wrong value, crashing, or wasting system resources. Roc packages also don't support build scripts, which was the vector used to successfully compromise the popular Rust arrayref package two months ago.
Portability. Roc pure functions are designed to be extremely deterministic: they always return the same values when given the same arguments—not just when run on the same machine, but also on any target you compile that code to. (The functions may also crash or fail to terminate, but that behavior should also be deterministic across targets.) The only way a Roc pure function should be expected to behave differently when run on two different systems is if one system runs out of memory mid-execution.
If any of these guarantees don't hold in practice, it can only be due to a defect in Roc's compiler, the platform the application is running on, or the underlying hardware. So when you see in roc-deflate's docs that the entire package is 100% pure functions, you can be confident you are getting all of the above properties from everything the package has to offer. The type system enforces it!
The reason we've been working so hard on all this might become clearer if you look at the proposition in reverse: would you give up guaranteed memory safety, guaranteed lack of side effects, guaranteed deterministic behavior across all targets, and the security benefits of having no exploitable build scripts in packages...for an average speedup percentage in the single digits?
That answer can legitimately vary by use case—Roc's own compiler, for example, wants the maximum performance the hardware can deliver—but I bet a lot of people reading this can see why we're so excited to have achieved this result.
Roc-Specific Optimizations
Most of the optimizations that improved roc-deflate's numbers came from general optimization techniques that are widely beneficial across languages. (I always recommend Casey Muratori's Performance-Aware Programming Series, which I paid for and learned a lot from.) Some of the optimization techniques were Roc-specific, though, and I wanted to mention them here as a reference for others. Even if you're not writing Roc code, this can also give you an idea of how Roc achieves its performance.
Avoid Unnecessary Sharing
One of Roc's most effective optimizations is opportunistic mutation (which Koka calls "Functional but In-Place"). You can learn how it works in Roc's docs on opportunistic mutation, but from a performance optimization perspective, it's critically important to avoid unnecessary sharing so that values remain unique and therefore eligible for in-place mutation.
Hoist Bounds Checks
You can't opt out of bounds checks (e.g. getting a value out of a dynamically-sized collection) in Roc like you can in C, Zig, and Rust, but Roc's compiler can optimize them away if it knows they'd be guaranteed to pass. Bounds checks are most costly inside loops, so you can get a lot of mileage out of adding something like if collection.len() <= highest_index_used { return 0 } before the loop starts. This adds an additional check that looks redundant, but it can allow the optimizer to safely delete costlier checks inside the loop, once it can tell that failures would not be reachable after that early return.
Build Lookup Tables at Compile Time
Roc's compile-time evaluation can be used to assemble lookup tables at compile time as long as nothing depends on runtime inputs. Even better, since their lengths are known at compile time, you can do things like Ok(entry) = lookup_table.get(5) to do an exhaustive pattern match that Roc's compiler will know is valid thanks to compile-time evaluation. This avoids runtime bounds checks that non-constant tables might have to pay for.
Consider Wrapping Arithmetic
In Roc, a + b desugars to a.plus(b). For an integer like U64, U64.plus includes an overflow check, whereas plus_wrap does not. Although plus is the safer default, overflow checks have a runtime cost, as CPUs can do wrapping integer arithmetic in one instruction. When Roc's compiler can prove that overflow won't occur, both plus and plus_wrap will optimize to the same instructions, but when it can't, you may get a speedup by choosing plus_wrap.
Room for Improvement
I'm sure there are still opportunities to improve roc-deflate's performance—especially on x64 CPUs—as well as the optimization pipeline in Roc's compiler.
At this point I feel reasonably confident that all the low-hanging fruit has been picked, but if anyone wants to try it out for themselves, here's the script I ran to set up and run the benchmark suite on Linux. (Note that Claude Opus 5.5 generated this script, and I haven't vetted it for security; run it outside a sandbox at your own risk!) It pins both Roc compiler revisions and roc-deflate versions, so you'll want to adjust those commits if you're trying out potential improvements.
For my part, I'll be focusing on the upcoming Roc 0.1.0 release from now until it's out. It's been eight years in the making, so I'll be very happy for us to finally have a numbered release! If you'd like to learn more about Roc, check out roc-lang.org or come say hi on Roc Zulip!

THE NETWORK
Emergency Action Messages are the coded traffic of the US nuclear forces, read aloud in the phonetic alphabet on the High Frequency Global Communications System. The primary frequency is 11175 kHz, upper sideband, and anyone with a shortwave radio can hear it.
Why shortwave? HF bounces off the ionosphere, so one transmitter reaches thousands of miles with nothing in between. Its weakness is the same sky: a nuclear burst floods the ionosphere with electrons and HF gets absorbed instead of reflected. So HFGCS is one path among several. It's the one you can hear, and because every message is encrypted, hearing it is all anyone outside the force can do.

THE CAPSULE
The messages you can hear above are meant for rooms like this one. The capsule is where an EAM lands: a command post passes it down, the console takes it in, and the crew acts on it. If an order to launch ever came, this is how it would arrive.
Sixty feet down, behind an eight-ton blast door, two officers sit a 24-hour alert in a room the size of a school bus.
The crew commander sits left, the deputy right. Between them: the launch control console, the printers, the phones, and the shelf of procedures that governs every minute.
A missile combat crew on alert. The red clock above the binders keeps Zulu time — the time every message to the capsule is written in. The crew checks it every day against the U.S. Naval Observatory's master clock, to the second.
Clock detail: Daniel Frenkel, 321st Missile Squadron, 2012–2016.

BINDER 4
THE CREW
A missile combat crew is two officers, a commander and a deputy. They go to the field together, take the capsule over from the crew before them, and hold it for 24 hours.
The day has a shape.
When a message comes in, both officers have to agree it is authentic before anything else happens.
A flight commander, left, and a deputy flight commander of the 10th Missile Squadron check their communications equipment at a launch control center near Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana, 16 March 2015.
U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Dillon Johnston, 341st Missile Wing Public Affairs. VIRIN 150316-F-HA826-128. Public domain.
A missile combat crew commander, 319th Missile Squadron, and her deputy commander simulate key turns of the Minuteman III weapon system in the E-01 Launch Control Center, F.E. Warren Air Force Base missile complex, Wyoming, 9 February 2016.
U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Jason Wiese, 90th Missile Wing. VIRIN 160209-F-BR137-127. Public domain.
FROM THE MESSAGE TO THE KEYS
1THE MESSAGE
An order reaches the capsule as an emergency action message, an EAM. A command post passes the coded message to the launch control centers under it. In the capsule the message comes in through the console's communications element, which handles messages from higher authority and processes emergency action messages. It is the same kind of message you can copy above.
Sources: HD 2001 p. 7 · HD 2001 p. 3 · REACT fact sheet
2AUTHENTICATE
Before acting, the crew has to authenticate the message. Only when both officers agree the message is authentic do they go on.
Sources: NPS HRS p. 115 · HD 2001 p. 7
3TWO OFFICERS, TWO KEYS
The system was built so that no single person could launch a missile. A crew is two officers, a commander and a deputy, and each has a launch key. In the Cold War capsule preserved at Delta-01, the two key switches were 12 feet apart. The console is the REACT system, fitted in 1995 and 1996. In the 2016 photograph above, the two officers sit side by side at the console, each at their own panel; the Air Force caption says they are simulating key turns. The launch switches are on separate panels of that console, and the keys are still turned together.
Sources: NPS HRS p. 85 · HAER CO-84 p. 10 · NMUSAF "Missile Combat Crews" · SAC guide p. 7 · NPS TwHP, Reading 3 · HD 2001 pp. 20, 24 · DVIDS 2406843 · DVIDS 2991929 · HD 2001 p. 7
4TWO CAPSULES
One crew's keys are not enough, because the system was also built so that no single crew could launch. Normally a second capsule has to vote as well. Without that corroborating signal from another launch control center, the missile does not launch.
Sources: NPS HRS p. 85 · HD 2001 p. 7 · DVIDS 2406843 · DVIDS 2991929 · NPS HRS p. 115
5WHAT A CAPSULE REACHES
Each capsule has primary control of the ten missiles in its flight. Five flights make a squadron of 50, and each of its five capsules can command and monitor all 50. Today the force is 400 Minuteman III missiles in three wings: F.E. Warren in Wyoming, Malmstrom in Montana and Minot in North Dakota.
Sources: HD 2001 p. 7 · NPS HRS p. 28 · AF LGM-30G fact sheet, current as of February 2019
6HOW MANY?
That's in the order. Nobody outside the force knows, and we don't guess.

All the Airmen going to the field that day are briefed on road conditions, weather, maintenance, the security status of the launch facilities and more. It can take 15 minutes or an hour and a half; mission planning by squadron follows.

title: “We should be more ambitious with the software we build”
content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying
[W]e should be more ambitious1 with the software we build
There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader2, this money overflow bug, etc.
This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free3, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.
That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).
As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.
But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.
If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.
Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:
Ripgrep
Compiling Rust
Syscall and filesystem overhead
At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now.
For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.
My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now4.
Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.
When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher)5.
For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats6.
BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle7. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing8. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.
Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.
I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.
I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that woudl be a super interestin thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago.
Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build
Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):
If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think
I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover
My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.
And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with

title: How Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
content:
OCT 22 2026
How we deploy Trillion-parameter frontier models on Cerebras
SARAH CHIENG
One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.
In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.
We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.
By the end, you'll understand:
How we fit the full model into on-chip memory
How we map the model across multiple chips
How we handle a high # of concurrent requests
Breaking it down with Kimi K3
Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.
It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here.
For this illustrative example, we use:
A 256k assumed average request size
4-bit weight quantization (like the Hugging Face implementation)
An 8-bit KV cache
#1: Size of Each layer
To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer.
Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is:
Dividing that payload by 93 layers then gives:
#2: Number of Wafers
Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type:
Dense layers need additional room for a KV cache, because each dense (full-attention) layer stores the keys and values for every token in every active request. So, we place one dense layer per wafer and leave the remaining SRAM for its KV cache.
Linear-attention layers do not require additional room for a KV cache. Instead of storing keys and values for every token, a linear-attention layer keeps a small, fixed-size state per request, regardless of context length. That leaves room for two linear layers per wafer (2 × 16 GB = 32 GB).
Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers, we get:
This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers.
#3: Connecting the wafers together
Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.
It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.
This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.
#4: How we serve 1 request
Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.
For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.
#5: How we serve many requests
This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?
No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.
While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.

To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.
#6: How many requests can we serve?
The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.
For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with:
Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case:
Calculating the # of Concurrent Requests
To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up:
To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide:
The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously.
Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed.
How this scales beyond 3T parameters
The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.

title: How Japanese Dried Bonito Is Made
content:
posted 5d ago by Jason Kottke
How Japanese Dried Bonito Is Made
This workshop founded in 1882 still makes dried bonito like they did back in the Edo period.
How katsuobushi — Japanese dried bonito, said to be the world’s hardest food — is made in Nishi-Izu, Japan. Inside Kanesa Katsuobushi Shoten, a workshop founded in 1882, 5th-generation craftsman Yasuhisa Serizawa still uses the 200-year-old “tebiyama” hand-fired smoke-drying method that only a few workshops in Japan preserve. Watch fresh bonito being filleted and boiled for 90 minutes, smoke-dried more than 10 times over a hand-tended wood fire, repaired with bonito paste, fermented with koji mold and sun-dried for months — over half a year until the fish becomes as hard as wood and shines like a jewel. From fresh catch to katsuobushi.
Check out Kanesa Katsuobushi Shoten’s website for more info; here’s what they say about the tebiyama drying/smoking method (Google translation):
This method of making dried bonito flakes has been used in the Tago district of West Izu for a long time, and its history is said to date back about 300 years (to the Edo period). It involves digging a vertical hole about 2 meters deep, burning firewood (raw wood from Izu: oak, sawtooth oak, cherry, etc.) from the bottom of the hole, and smoking and drying the dried bonito flakes with the high temperature of an open flame. This method is called the Tebiyama-shiki smoking method. It is the oldest existing smoking method, and only a few bonito flake manufacturers in the country continue to use this method to make dried bonito flakes, so it is said to be a legendary method. The Tebiyama-shiki smoking method is said to produce dried bonito flakes with a rich flavor because the surface of the bonito is smoked all at once with the high temperature of an open flame, locking in the umami.

title: Small Programs and Languages - ratfactor
content:
This is a card in Dave's Virtual Box of Cards.
Small Programs and Languages
Page started: 2025-06-02
Page published: 2026-07-28
My Implementing a Forth article got some great feedback, particularly around the subject of tiny Forth implementations. (And it was an excuse to list some of the tiniest Forths I’ve seen.)
I know I’m not alone in seeing the appeal of tiny Forths, tiny languages, tiny programs, and just small stuff in general. What’s up with that, anyway?
The appeal of tiny programs
Tiny programs are approachable.
If I see that something is 200 lines of code, I’m much more likely to read it than if it’s 2,000 or 20,000 lines.
What’s more, if it’s a program that does something interesting in 20 lines when I was expecting 2,000, then I’m going to be very, very interested to read those 20 lines!
When I was researching DOM diffing libraries prior to creating RetroV, one of the repos I looked at was ijk by Luke Jackson.
I was pretty used to looking at fat JavaScript libraries at that point, so when I cracked open the source file for ijk, I was really surprised. Here’s the source: index.js (githubusercontent.com).
Just 25 lines! I was instantly intrigued.
More recently, one of the responses to my aforementioned Forth article was Philippe Brochard with a 46 byte "Forth".
46 bytes!
It’s so small, I can just put the hexdump right here:
50b8 8e00 31d8 e8ff 0017 003c 0575 00ea
5000 3c00 7401 eb02 e8ee 0005 0588 eb47
b8e6 0200 d231 14cd e480 7580 c3f4
(See my update to Implementing a Forth for more about this artifact.)
Sure, very few people jump at a chance to read raw machine code. But that’s exactly my point. Something this small doesn’t feel so scary, right? I mean, 46 bytes. If you put the effort into it, you know you can figure out how it works eventually.
This next one almost serves as a counter-example because the code is so dense and frightening, but I can’t help mentioning it anyway.
One of my favorite software stories is Roger K.W. Hui’s Appendix A "Incunabulum" from An Implementation of J in which he describes Arthur Whitney writing an array-based language interpreter,
"…on one page and in one afternoon — an interpreter fragment on the AT&T 3B1 computer. I studied this interpreter for about a week for its organization and programming style…"
Hui can list the entire interpreter in the appendix because it’s just that single page, 122 lines of incredibly cryptic C, which you can view here:
https://code.jsoftware.com/wiki/Essays/Incunabulum
I haven’t personally tackled that puzzle yet, but it’s in my unwritten list of dense computer things that I would print out and take with me if I suddenly found myself cast out of society and forced to go live alone up on a mountain or something.
(By the way, J is in the family of array languages which include APL. If you enjoy brevity, cryptic programming puzzles, and high performance numerical computing, these languages have got you covered!)
Update July 2026: Speaking of Arthur Whitney, Alex (alexalejandre.com) sent me a link that I knew I’d have to add here. Check this out: https://fall.tr/kos
It’s a transcript of a Geo Carncross talk describing an operating system, kOS, featuring Whitney’s k array language, kdb database, and a GUI and window manager in a 90 Kb bootable image. Individual source code stats are just as impressive (such as 60 lines of C for the aforementioned GUI and window manager). And apparently kdb is 100 lines of C? Is that right? Even Whitney C, that’s still impressive. Now I’m even more intrigued by kdb than ever! And if any of that seems interesting, you’ll definitely enjoy the article Impending kOS (vector.org.uk).
Something else that would certainly need to be in the collection I take to that lonely mountain would have to be The Most Beautiful Program Ever Written, according to the title of a talk by William Byrd. Spoiler alert: It’s this Lisp interpreter in Lisp:
(define eval-expr
  (lambda (expr env)
    (pmatch expr
      [`,x (guard (symbol? x))
        (env x)]
      [`(lambda (,x) ,body)
        (lambda (arg)
          (eval-expr body (lambda (y)
                            (if (eq? x y)
                                arg
                                (env y)))))]
      [`(,rator ,rand)
       ((eval-expr rator env)
        (eval-expr rand env))])))
(The above is from Alberto Zaccagni’s transcription of the code (github.com) shown in Byrd’s slide.)
Recreation or fundamental truths?
Now, we all know that code golfing (wikipedia.org) is a programmer’s recreational game, and just for fun, right?
But is any of this actually useful?
I say yes. And I’ll go one step further: They are meaningful.
When you see a ray tracer that fits on a business card (fabiensanglard.net), it makes you realize that a ray tracer is something that can fit on a business card!
That’s an actual fact about the minimum complexity of ray tracers.
Kolmogorov complexity (wikipedia.org) is:
"…the length of a shortest computer program (in a predetermined programming language) that produces the object as output."
(I learned about Kolmogorov complexity in a book about Kurt Gödel and it was my favorite thing in what was otherwise a pretty dry and depressing book.)
The meaning I get from this is that code golfers, for the benefit of the whole human race, produce versions of programs that represent the minimum complexity of those programs. Way to go code golfers!
What do we know about the fundamental complexity of the Lisp programming language?
Thanks to Justine Tunney, we know that a LISP with garbage collection can be as small as 436 bytes (justine.lol).
That’s a fact about Lisps with garbage collection. When you strip everything else away, you can get the essentials down to 436 bytes!
I take comfort in this because that means the concept can be boiled down to this hand-held size. And that means I can probably fit it in my head.
Thanks to Frank Force, we know that a 3D browser game can fit in 2Kb of (insanely compressed) JavaScript source: A 3D game in 2Kb of JS (frankforce.com)
Martin Kleppe’s whole site (aem1k.com) is filled with wonders you can run right in your browser.
And we haven’t even scraped the surface of what the demoscene has to offer for computers going back to the 1980s. Here’s a good place to start: https://demoscene.assembly.org/
Mini-things are fun and useful and meaningful.
My point here is that you don’t have to actually study the intricate clockwork puzzle of a miniaturized/golfed program to benefit from it. The miniature simply serves to prove that the concept can fit on a business card and it can fit in your head. Go ahead and find a readable version to study instead. (The miniature will likely have many things to teach, but some of them will be about how to make miniature programs.)
Small languages
Small programs are interesting. But I’m also interested in small programming languages.
Generally speaking, the smaller the language, the less expressive it is.
One of the most well-known, least expressive languages is assembly.
Assembly languages are very syntactically and conceptually simple. There’s not much language at all: it’s mostly a rigid sequence of opcode mnemonics. Even with macros, writing in assembly is mostly about understanding the puzzle of a particular CPU’s instruction set architecture, or ISA. (You can prove this by comparing the syntax of assembly for CISC and RISC processors. The puzzle is totally different, while the language remains practically unchanged.)
An honorable mention must be made here for SNOBOL, which is kind of like assembly language both for the rigid syntactic reasons listed above and also because it presents a similar control flow challenge. Like a CPU, it only understands jumps and call/return. (In every other way, SNOBOL is wildly different, being a string matching and replacing language. It’s weird and fun and highly effective.)
Moving on to syntactically tiny "high-level" languages, these three are brilliant:
Forths win just about any "smallness" contest. The only syntactical construct is the space character. Forths are mind-bendingly flexible and powerful in a way that is downright disturbing.
Lisps, (especially Scheme?), have small core languages with very simple syntax and enormous expressive power and flexibility.
Tcl deserves to be mentioned with Forth and Lisp. Tcl is wild because everything is a string in a way that is hard to appreciate at first. You can construct your own language in Tcl just as you can with Forth or Lisp.
Forth, Lisp, and Tcl only require you to understand a few core ideas and give you limitless power in return. You could fit the syntactic core of these languages on an index card or less.
And yet, to wield these tools effectively requires a massive shift in thinking if you’re used to "normal" Algol-like procedural languages.
So how about something that is both small and simple and doesn’t require a blood sacrifice?
I think the Lua programming language fits the bill. Check out how small the core language is:
https://lua.org/manual/5.1/
I’ve got the printed book version of this document and it’s a thin book! The Lua language is covered in the beginning and it is just 27 pages. 27 pages! I have game manuals longer than that.
The C language is pretty small. I don’t think it’s super easy to program effectively and safely with C, but there’s no denying it’s compact and pretty expressive for its size.
Newcomer Zig is C-like. But I think it’s actually quite large and you need to know a lot of it to use it effectively. (I’m also a fan of Zig and think it’s totally worth it. The size is there for a reason.)
JavaScript has a core language that is quite small. Probably on par with Lua, actually. Functions, arrays, and objects (used as dictionaries) are pretty much all the JS I use and I like it that way!
As with the natural human languages, the trade-off with a bigger programming language is, hopefully, greater expressivity.
Small or expressive. Which way should you lean?
In a wonderful talk by David Ungar (wikipedia.org) titled Self and Self: Whys and Wherefores, he laments the mistake of Self’s multiple inheritance:
"It’s far better to make a system a little too simple so a person has to write extra stuff, even write it twice with a comment that says, 'Look over here,' than to have a system that acts in strange ways and nobody can understand why. So, simplicity trumps expressiveness."
Got that? Here’s the bullet from the slide to help you remember:
I think small languages can also be fairly expressive, but only with very, very careful design. Recall Forth, Lisp, and Tcl.
Microworlds: The idea of small, self-contained, learnable programming environments also has a David Ungar connection I discovered while watching his talk. See "ARK" on my Microworlds card. (Smith and Ungar co-created the Self language (selflanguage.org), which is a notable milestone in programming and still under active development to this day.)
Languages which come with full-featured interactive IDEs are obvious potential microworlds.
But I also think that traditional text file-based programming can give you the microworld experience as well. For that, a language needs high quality documentation that installs alongside the compiler/interpreter. And it should strive to have error output that can be understood by beginners, including explanations of what went wrong and hints for how to fix it or or where to find more information.
Libraries: Another easily overlooked aspect of a programming language’s apparent size is its "standard library" of functions, data structures, and methods.
I think function libraries are subject to the exact same size versus expressiveness challenge.
For example, learning the Ramda (ramdajs.com) functional programming library for JavaScript was very much like learning a new programming language and I never managed to learn all of it. The composability of Ramda and the consistency of its curried functions was extremely eye-opening to me. My advice: A little bit of Ramda goes a long way!
The feels: Concision in our tools has a certain quality that goes beyond utility. Little things just spark joy, you know?
Why are small things so delightful?
The appeal of tiny things in general
I’ve always had a fascination with miniatures, dioramas, and tiny scale models.
I know I’m not alone!
Stephanie M. Langin-Hooper, author of Figurines in Hellenistic Babylonia writes in Tiny Things and Why We Love Them (cambridgeblog.org):
"…the act of shrinking a life-size thing to a smaller scale has an influential effect. The object is now cute, more accessible, more delicate, more 'squee'. It is also more helpless, and thus controllable – comforting and completely non-threatening due to its diminutive size.
Which is exactly the reaction I have when I see a tiny bit of code that does something useful.
Also, I’m super okay with "controllable" in the context of a computer, but the feeling of that paragraph changes a bit if we’re talking about, say, dolls.
Small scale helps make "big" things approachable:
"What might be threatening to think about in the real-scale world can be more manageable and more conceivable in miniature."
Small things, "allow low-stakes experimentation," which is why we often build tiny models of things before we scale them up.
Simon Garfield, author of In Miniature: How Small Things Illuminate the World has many of the same answers. He writes in Small world: Why we love tiny things (theguardian.com):
"The answer lies in our desire for mastery and elucidation. The ability to enhance a life by bringing scaled-down order and illumination to an otherwise chaotic world – a world over which we may otherwise feel we have little control – cannot be overvalued. […] At its simplest, the miniature shows us how to see, learn and appreciate more with less."
I think this is a big part of what I get out of Assembly Nights with the small scale and orderly logic and internal consistency. Unlike the vast, fathomless Real World, an offline computer is a fantasy place where I can believe I could understand everything if I just tried hard enough for long enough.
"The satisfaction of observing small things becomes a desire to make small things, and both stages address the human need for comprehension and order. We live in a huge and doomy universe, and controlling just a tiny scaled-down part of it restores our sense of order and worth."
I’ve been studying computer history for a little while and I’ve only scratched the surface. But one of the things I’ve been finding is that a lot of the "big" stuff in our field are just accumulations of lots of "little" victories as individuals have solved "little" problems in new and different ways.
"We create small universes in which we may bury ourselves to the exclusion of all else. Blocking out real life for a while – always the prerequisite of the dedicated domestic hobby, from doll’s house modeller to jigsaw enthusiast to adult book colourist – may be contemplative, meditative, blinkered and

title: Gopher
content:
Entry 001 - Why gopher in 2026?

May 22nd 2026

First off, if you're reading this, you're probably the kind of person who can't
just use a tool, you have to know how it works. There are smart people who are
good at what they do. Some people are master chefs, awesome mechanics, great
sculptors or skillful accountants. But how many of those people dive so deep
into what they are good at to understand what makes it tick?

People like us are the ones who build a phlog for fun just to get a feeling for
how far we've come with technology. Maybe you're here for the nostalgia, maybe
it's to turn off the noise of modern tech. The important part is you are here
now, in 2026 or beyond.

I'm noticing a trend with my 17 year old and their friends with ADHD where they
want to turn off the noise of the world and go back to simpler times. As one
who is from those simpler times, I'm a little proud but also a little "Get off
my lawn!" It's impossible to go back to that at this point and for better or
worse, we have to make sense of where we are. Flip phones are simple and low-
tech to them, but for us they were the latest in tech!

We have syntax highlighting in vim that wasn't there when I was using vi so
many years ago. Now I not only know it's there, but I can google how to set up
so many features that I didn't know existed and would never figure out from the
manual. Back in the day you had to find someone who first off knew what you
were even talking about and second who knew more than you did. For me, this was
how I ended up knowing a little about a lot but not being able to wrestle the
arcane knowledge from the man pages.

I think tech is in a weird place that is both super helpful and yet so
unhelpful at the same time. Subscriptions for everything, services changing
all the time and profits driving the direction of everything. It's nice to find
a place like sdf that operates like how things used to.

Thanks for stopping by!
Wayne

===============================================================================

2026 May 24, 10:29

I feel you, on one hand we cant go back, on the other, we have
to go back. Im not sure where that leaves us. All I know is that
I (myself) need to slow down. - y4my4m

content:

AI and the Fall? of the Creative Class
America is Losing Hundreds of Thousands of Jobs in Media, Film & the Arts. How Much is AI to Blame?
JOSEPH POLITANO
SEP 27, 2026
268
58
52
Share
Thanks for reading! If you haven’t subscribed, please click the button below:
Subscribe
By subscribing, you’ll join over 80,000 people who read Apricitas!
America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone. That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008. Yet there’s no generalized recession today—instead, this period of job loss coincides with the rise of AI systems that can compose wholesale novels, photorealistic images, soundalike music, and practically every other form of digital art, en masse and at extremely low costs. Is this the fall of the Creative Class?
Proving the exact amount of AI-driven job loss in the arts is extremely difficult. Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights. The effects of AI are also hard to disentangle from other factors currently affecting arts businesses, like consolidation in Hollywood, offshoring of content production, or the continued displacement of traditional media providers in favor of social media creators. Yet perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.
Some of those digital job losses are just a continuation of prior trends, like in the publishing industry where technological change has been continually grinding away newspaper and magazine jobs for decades. Yet for sectors like live broadcasting, streaming, or graphic design, recent experience is an unusual downturn compared to the tranquility of years prior. Then there’s the worst-hit sector, movie & sound recording, which has been bleeding jobs at a nearly unprecedented pace over the last three years.
Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total. At the depths touched this summer, total employment was lower than at any point since the 2008 recession and approaching the lowest point in 30 years. The streaming era has proven an extremely difficult transition, with traditional films and TV shows losing watch time to user-generated and increasingly AI-assisted or AI-generated content flows.
Overall, nearly half the media job losses of the last four years have been concentrated in the movie & sound recording sector that includes Hollywood. Written publishing has been the next-largest source of job loss, with employment down by more than 70k over the same time frame. Yet the job losses have by no means been contained to any particular part of media; instead they’ve hit nearly every subsector at some point. Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months. Will further AI development continue displacing workers in creative industries?
Subscribe
Can the Arts Business Model Survive?
To understand what could happen to the business of art amidst the rise of AI, it’s important to understand what did happen to it during the first digital transition, the rise of the internet.
It was the turn of the millennium, and Metallica had a problem. Demos of their upcoming, unreleased tracks were bouncing around radio and the internet, originally leaked onto a new internet file-sharing website called Napster. There they found thousands of files shared amongst hundreds of thousands of users, many of which were direct rips of albums that sold for $15 being offered for free. The most anticipated albums were often leaked online even before they were on store shelves. Metallica sued Napster for copyright infringement, and they were soon joined by separate suits from other prominent artists and eventually the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).
Much of the general public was understandably unsympathetic to Metallica, perceived as a bunch of already-successful millionaires trying to bilk even more money from listeners, and were even less sympathetic towards the RIAA, perceived as scurrilous middlemen who take from artists and fans alike. But the two of them easily won their lawsuit, forcing Napster into bankruptcy. Yet Metallica may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.
The modern internet made file-sharing extremely easy, and no matter how much whac-a-mole companies played, they could not possibly catch every illegal upload. The perennial threat of piracy undermined their copyright and limited their ability to charge for music. Eventually, the value of individual songs fell to the point that companies like Spotify and Apple Music could swoop in to acquire massive catalogues, consolidate them, and charge a comparatively trivial fee for access. For what a single Metallica album would have cost in 2000, you can now get a month’s worth of unlimited access to nearly all human-made music.
The music industry has never returned to the heyday paydays of the peak CD era—even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales. This was a massive boon to consumers, but it was also a squeeze on musicians that forced them to fundamentally change their business model over time. Instead of just selling records to earn money directly, music itself increasingly became a loss-leading advertisement for the live concerts (and merch) that provided a growing share of artists’ income. Tours got longer, venues got bigger, ticket prices skyrocketed, and musicians frequently took on roles closer to public influencers than isolated artistes. Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.
Of course, there were still significant downsides to the transition into the streaming era. Bands (especially smaller ones) complain about the unending pressure to always be on tour. Musicians whose content was suited to home listening lost out to those more suited to giant festivals. Even accounting for concert revenues, musicians made less money than before. Yet musicians fared better than many areas of entertainment subsectors because there was a live component to fall back on—for many media industries, the digital era left no such comfort.
Over time, the business of video has moved in the opposite direction of music—out of the theatre and into the home. Hollywood formerly made most of its money enticing customers to visit sold-out movie theatres, but these were gradually supplanted by broadcast TV, cable, and physical media. Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval. That is, until the modern streaming era.
Today, the plethora of video options and the rise of social media have sent video producers into a vicious competition for limited attention. Even before adjusting for inflation, movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop. The mountain of free user-generated content on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, or social media was already presenting harsh competition for traditional video companies in the years before ChatGPT’s launch, and now streaming services are also competing with a flood of AI-generated content. The business model of video media is fundamentally getting squeezed, and unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.
The actual worst-case scenario for creative workers amidst the AI revolution is something similar to what happened to the publishing industry after the advent of the internet—that is, near-total collapse of their fundamental business model. Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping. Magazine publishers likewise have let 66% of their staff go since the 90s, while book publishers have lost 40%.
The routine informational updates that previously formed newspapers’ bread-and-butter were all de-bundled—box scores moved to sports websites, stock movements went to financial websites, forecasts went to weather websites—each loss compounding on itself to undermine consumers’ need to buy the paper. Search engines became the first place people looked to for information, and newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead. The collective of social media users became faster at breaking any news story than a daily paper could ever hope to be. When papers eventually did start aggressively paywalling content, the internet made it trivially easy for people to just copy the articles’ content and share it beyond the paywall. The entire business model had collapsed, to the point that now only a select few major newspapers can even survive.
That scale of copyright dilution and forced unbundling is the worst-case scenario for media businesses in the age of AI. It’s possible arts jobs could survive via consumers’ deep-seated aversion to explicitly AI-generated content, but AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer. Roughly 32% of workers in the overall arts, entertainment, and recreation sector use Generative AI to some extent, which is less than the 62% average across all industries, but still enough that virtually every major media project could have some AI within its workflow.
Indeed, AI is likely seeping into media production processes in ways large companies themselves would struggle to prevent even when they desire to—how can a TV studio be sure nobody in their writers’ room is consulting ChatGPT for jokes or any storyboard artist is generating concept art? And even if professional TV and movie studios do effectively hold out against temptation and prevent internal AI use, how long can they compete with the large mass of wannabe independent creators with much fewer scruples? Plenty of media businesses tried to hold out against the algorithmic content waves of the 2010s and were buried as a result.
Subscribe
Conclusions
Yet fundamentally, it’s difficult to meaningfully predict how new technologies will interact with existing arts businesses. Take the unexpected resurgence in book sales over the last four years. The novel as a commercial art form had been struggling for decades, with fewer books sold in 2019 than at the beginning of the millennium, but the last six years have seen an unprecedented 70% surge in sales. The unlikely savior of the printed word came from perhaps its polar opposite—TikTok.
Of course, fewer people read now than ever before—for the general public, short-form video apps have accelerated the displacement of reading, just as TV, video games, or social media before them. Yet for a dwindling number of dedicated repeat readers, “BookTok” became a new way to source reviews, analysis, discourse, and community in a way that boosted the reading experience and absolutely turbocharged book sales. It’s possible that AI tools could have those same totally unpredictable spillovers for other museums, concerts, or other forms of art in ways that are unpredictable today, in much the same way short-form video saved books in ways that could never have been anticipated beforehand.
At the end of the day, the arts are only a small sector of the overall macroeconomy. Media made up a small share of the labor market even at its peak, and it has always been difficult to get hired in creative industries to the point that making fun of art students’ job prospects became an easy punchline. The movie industry has an income profile closer to eggs or bicycles than something major like healthcare or finance. Were the goal to create art for art’s sake, for the intangible and nonmonetizable cultural benefits, it would be relatively easy to counterbalance any economic impacts of AI on artists just by reversing recent cuts to the National Endowments for the Arts & Humanities.
It’s telling that Anthropic, the most prominent AI lab, has basically never bothered with image, video, or music generation, because the prospective economic benefits are marginal when compared to using AI to tackle math or scientific problems. OpenAI learned this lesson the hard way when it was forced to abandon its video generation platform Sora, deciding it had better use for its limited compute than making synthetic TikToks. Nowadays, the art generation is done primarily by secondary players running smaller models, though even these are large enough to threaten significant disruption to legacy media businesses.
In other words, the primary impacts of AI art will be on culture and society rather than the macroeconomy. Yet arts jobs might be a microcosm for other “creative-adjacent” work that occupies a much larger share of economic activity. Take the tech sector itself, which is the clearest place where AI-driven job loss has shown up outside the media business, as powerful coding agents replace human programmers. Annual tech job gains stood at nearly 300k in 2022, but the sector has been bleeding jobs every year since then in what is now its longest labor market downturn.
Right now, AI-driven job displacement has been relatively minor outside of these few narrow sectors. Unemployment is higher than it was four years ago but still below even the 2010s average, and overall job turnover rates remain extremely low. Some white-collar sectors that looked prime for AI automation have even been on a hiring spree over the last few years, including legal and engineering firms. Yet if the economic impact of AI ends up being anywhere near large enough to validate the trillions of dollars investors are currently betting on it, these economic disruptions will only spread from here.

title: I Built a Stereo Vision Board for Hardware Hackers - Rootkit Labs Blog
content:
This article was written entirely by a human, for humans.
I tend to get excited about certain chips. This time, it was a microprocessor: The Rockchip RV1103 is a single-core 1.1 GHz ARM Cortex-A7 SoC (system on chip) with 64 MB of DDR2 RAM and a MIPI CSI-2 bus shoved into a QFN-88 package. With this chip, I built a cheap, simple stereo vision board with built-in compute and Linux support.
Design Files
I envision integrating this board into robotics projects, like an Arduino needing obstacle avoidance or navigation. Once powered up, the board transmits data over serial. Or you can use it on its own, with everything you’d expect from a Linux board.
The video below shows image capture and depth processing on the hardware:
This blog post outlines the hardware, firmware, and software details!
System Overview
The PCB
A cheap four-layer board worked for this project.
Top Layer: Controlled-impedance traces: USB, MIPI, and Ethernet. With some Signal/Power.
Inner L1: Solid ground.
Inner L2: Signal/Power
Bottom Layer: Signal/Power
I got the board mostly correct on the first shot, but there were a few issues:
I requested the wrong SoC. That was a fun replacement.
The holes for the lens mounts were drilled at 1.8 mm instead of 2.2 mm.
1k resistors were too small to make the LEDs light up nicely.
The 0.9 V trace was too thin, although it seemed to work fine.
The Kernel, Bootloader, and OS
I needed a bootable OS, with drivers, a bootloader and a kernel. For this I used my favorite Linux build system: Buildroot. Buildroot combines these elements into sdcard.img, which you flash to an SD card, pop into the board, and boot.
Sadly, not everything needed for this project is available upstream. The Rockchip MIPI drivers, hardware accelerators, and some other key components all came from the vendor BSP. Buildroot has support for out-of-tree kernels.
For this chip, there are a few different boot stages. Most ARM MPUs look something like this:
(Bootloader) BootROM: Gets TPL and runs it. This is in ROM and uses SRAM (smaller, non-main RAM).
(Bootloader) TPL (“Tertiary Program Loader”): Sets up the DRAM controller. This is a binary from Rockchip.
(Bootloader) SPL (“Secondary Program Loader”): Loads U-Boot, bundled with the U-Boot project.
(Bootloader) U-Boot: This is our main bootloader; it loads the kernel. It has other fancy features.
(Kernel): Linux
(OS) Init System: Starts services.
After some simple config in Buildroot, I had access to a shell over serial. I eventually moved to SSH, with the USB-C port as an Ethernet adapter.
The Software Stack
The software MVP needed to communicate with the kernel to get image data, control the camera, and use the hardware accelerators. Luckily, everything in the kernel space marked above was assembled for us with Buildroot. We just needed to make the blue part, but I’ll explain the rest briefly.
Kernel Space
You may notice drivers get more abstract at the top of the diagram, while lower down they’re hardware specific. This means a user application can talk to a node created by V4L2 and doesn’t need to care about specific camera commands.
There are SoC-specific drivers for the SoC peripherals (like I2C, CSI, etc.). This is so the camera driver (OV9281 in our case) doesn’t need to know which SoC it’s running on.
This is all pretty standard Linux device driver stuff, so I won’t go into any more details beyond this.
User Space
The data eventually flows up to Video4Linux2, which exposes our cameras in various nodes /dev/videoX. Each camera shows 11 video nodes:
video0: Normal video capture
video1-3: Other stream IDs
video4-7: Scalers
video8-10: Auxiliary tools
Camera control is exposed through /dev/v4l-subdevX. We can use these nodes to set exposure and control various camera features.
The “Rockchip Video Engine” is exposed through /dev/rve. We use the proprietary librve.a to talk with the engine and schedule various hardware video acceleration tasks. I’ll get more into this later.
The userspace app…
Configures the cameras from /dev/v4l-subdevX
Takes the image data from /dev/videoX
Feeds it into the /dev/rve node
The Rockchip Video Engine contains a SAD engine (sum of absolute differences). This is a hardware accelerator block that runs on the Rockchip SoC itself.
SAD is the core of how we do stereoscopic vision. A grayscale image can be represented as a matrix, with each element being a number from 0 to 255. Let’s say we have 2x images that are 2 × 2 px each. We can calculate the SAD:
Image 1  Image 2  Absolute differences
[10  20] [10  20] [0  0]
[30  40] [30  40] [0  0]

SAD = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0
We can say the two images are the same.
Now instead of comparing these tiny images, we have two big images and break them up into a bunch of smaller images, called patches, and do this everywhere.
Normalized SAD per patch (0 = identical).
We now have an algorithm to determine how similar patches of the image are, so with this information we can certainly say that this section of this image is different.
SAD-based stereo block matching uses the same principle, but compares a vertical column of patches after a horizontal shift. Our two images come from two separate cameras, separated horizontally by a distance we call the baseline. We keep one image fixed, shift the other, and try to find matching blocks; when the blocks match, this is a depth value. If they match at a very early shift, this is a far-away value, while a later shift is a closer image.
Stereo images: Middlebury Cones.
You can see that images farther away require less shifting to get a match, and once you get a match, the shifting required is your depth! The boxes show your patch size, and the green box is showing a SAD match. This is illustrated in this GIF above with three separate depths.
What’s Next?
I would like to sell a few of these devices and get some feedback.
If you’re interested in this device, please sign up for the email notification here. If I get more than 20 signups, I’ll order another 10 boards with all the fixes and list these for sale. Please note this isn’t a pre-order, but only sign up if you are serious about supporting the project :)
If I get enough interest, the next stage of the project will be software cleanups, image optimisations, implementing SLAM, and YOLO.
Thanks for reading!
