title: GitHub - Zagitta/gpu-unlock: Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents · GitHub
content:
GPU unlock 1.0.0
Unlock FP/BF16 instruction issue rate on Nvidia 3000's cards to their professional equivalents
This Linux kernel module combines the CMP unlocker's V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. It runs the unlock, writes the speed selectors (SS0 0x88888888, which selects the full BF16 rate, and the 4-bit SS1 0x8 IMLA4) and performs FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver.
The benefit of this early kmod driver is that it does not require manual patching each time nvidia releases a new driver version.
The effect of this unlock is that it doubles the instruction issuing speed of FP/BF16 FMA into FP32 operations on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards.
3090 Ti dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W, five-sample medians with FP32 accumulation:
Input Before After
FP16 87.46 TFLOPS 118.39 TFLOPS
BF16 87.50 TFLOPS 157.41 TFLOPS
TF32 42.58 TFLOPS 82.61 TFLOPS
Tested cards
Results reported by users. The module accepts every GeForce ID listed in kernel/gpu_unlock/main.c, but the cards below are the ones someone has reported on. Please add yours with a compatibility report, whether it worked or not.
Chip Card PCI ID Result BF16 GEMM gain Reports
GA102 RTX 3090 Ti 10de:2203 Unlocked +68–80% #1
GA102 RTX 3090 10de:2204 Unlocked +25–67% #5, #9, #10, #17, #25, #27, #33
GA102 RTX 3080 Ti 20 GB (OEM, GA102-250) 10de:2205 Unlock completes, BF16 stays at half rate — #28
GA102 RTX 3080 10 GB 10de:2206 Unlocked +70–73% #14
GA102 RTX 3080 20 GB (memory upgrade) 10de:2206 Unlocked +56–59% #10, #15
GA104 RTX 3070 10de:2484 Unlocked +73–81% #10, #12
GA104 RTX 3070 Ti 10de:2482 Not tested with this module (the same unlock worked from a UEFI port on Windows) — #32
GA106 RTX 3060 12 GB 10de:2504 Unlocked about +80% #13, #31
GA103 any 10de:2414 No reports yet — —
The gains are dense GEMM throughput from each report's own benchmark, so they are not directly comparable. The power limit matters a lot: the lowest figure (+25%) is from cards capped at 225 W.
Matrix-heavy work speeds up: LLM prefill (+14–36% in #9, #15, #25 and #33), diffusion and FlashAttention. LLM decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth, and INT8 work stay about the same. The reports that compared outputs found them bit-identical before and after.
Reports also cover up to four cards in one machine, the card driving the display, and cards passed through to a VM with vfio-pci (#17).
How to install
First run:
git clone https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
cd gpu-unlock
make install
Then append gpu_unlock.targets=all to your kernel command line, keeping existing options:
GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint): add it inside GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub, then run sudo update-grub.
GRUB (Arch/CachyOS): same edit, then run sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
Fedora/RHEL: run sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all".
systemd-boot: append it to the options line in your boot entry (bootctl status shows its location).
UKI / generated entries: add it to /etc/kernel/cmdline and regenerate your boot images/entries (e.g. sudo mkinitcpio -P for mkinitcpio UKIs).
Local build
Every build downloads the pinned NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS, checks their SHA-256, and generates firmware only in the build directory and the binary package. All three formats install through the same make install-* targets. Packages are built from the committed HEAD.
Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step (asks for your sudo password):
make install        # detect the distribution and select an installer
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf install
make install uses /etc/os-release (ID, then ID_LIKE) to detect Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, or Fedora/RHEL/CentOS families. The RPM installer requires DNF. For other distributions, select a compatible explicit target above.
make arch, make deb and make rpm only build. Debian and RPM packages go to build/deb and build/rpm. The NVIDIA inputs are cached in ~/.cache/gpu-unlock/inputs (make inputs; override with INPUTS=). dpkg-buildpackage itself never uses the network, so a clean-chroot build (sbuild or pbuilder) needs GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS pointing at that cache. The make dist archive, the Debian source package and the .nosrc.rpm contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware.
Boot flow and opt-in
The packages put gpu_unlock and its firmware in the initramfs and load it there, before nvidia can bind a card:
mkinitcpio: /etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf inserts gpu_unlock right before nvidia in MODULES, so a display card is blank for as short a time as possible. Without nvidia in the image, it goes last and still runs before an nvidia loaded from the root filesystem. Images are rebuilt on install. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image built with -c <config> or a preset _config; put gpu_unlock right before nvidia in that config's MODULES yourself.
initramfs-tools: /usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf.
dracut: /usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf.
With initramfs-tools and dracut, the module is built for every installed kernel that has headers, and those kernels' images are rebuilt on install and again on removal. Kernels installed later get the module and a new image from the kernel's own install hooks.
There is no softdep nvidia pre: rule: kmod honours only the first softdep nvidia line it reads, so other packages' rules (nvidia-utils, gddr6_hwmon) would silently override it, or it would override theirs.
The module does nothing unless the kernel command line opts in:
gpu_unlock.targets=all                          # every unbound GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0                 # only these cards
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0,0000:22:00.0    # comma-separated
Addresses are full PCI names as lspci -D prints them (hex digits in either case), independent of GPU numbering and display role. An entry that is not a GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 card, including all mixed with addresses, is logged and ignored. The cards are unlocked concurrently, about a second in all however many there are, and each on its own: a card that is already bound or powered down is skipped. Bus mastering that the board firmware left on (Supermicro X11 does this whatever its option ROM and bus master settings) is cleared first; a card some driver already initialised is still refused. Then nvidia loads and binds every card as usual.
The display card works too. Its firmware framebuffer (the boot console and Plymouth) keeps running while the unlock's firmware steps run, and is removed just before the card's reset, as nvidia-drm would do a moment later anyway. Its screen is blank from that reset until nvidia-drm takes over.
Loading the module by hand after boot does nothing to a card that nvidia has bound.
Suspend to RAM powers the cards off, which resets the speed selectors. After resume the module unlocks every card it unlocked at boot again, before nvidia resumes it: its suspend notifier runs just ahead of the one nvidia resumes its cards from (NVreg_UseKernelSuspendNotifiers=1, the default in current drivers; nvidia-resume.service runs later still). This adds about a second to resume. A card that kept power, as in suspend to idle, is still unlocked and is only read. A card that nvidia has already resumed, or that is bound to another driver, is left as it is, and the log says why. Add gpu_unlock.resume=0 to the kernel command line, or write 0 to /sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume, to turn this off. Hibernation is not covered.
Check the result with:
journalctl -k -b | grep gpu_unlock
lspci -nnk -s 0000:21:00.0
To stop unlocking, remove gpu_unlock.targets= from the kernel command line; for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.
If the firmware on a card never stops, the module logs it and keeps the DMA buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off before trying again.
The kernel module and local packaging are GPL-2.0-only. The generated payload derives from the pinned CMP reference; NVIDIA firmware remains under its own terms. See firmware/NOTICE.md and licenses/ for attribution and notices.

Developer repositories moved from GitHub to GitLab
jduval - Oct 15th, 2026
New home for developer resources will include open-source software for RSG 2.0 SDK, developer documentation repo, samples, and tools
Roku has completed migrating all developer resources from GitHub to GitLab. The move covers the developer documentation, sample apps, and the tooling repositories you build against, consolidating them into a single, central location.
The impact to developers is minimal:
Links in the developer documentation and blog posts have been updated to the new GitLab URLs, so following a link from our docs lands you in the right place.
If you’ve bookmarked or stored a Roku repository URL, you’ll need to update it.
Updating your bookmarked URLs
The repository names are staying the same; therefore, a repository at github.com/rokudev/<repo> is now at gitlab.com/rokudev/<repo>. Anywhere you have bookmarked or stored a Roku repository URL, you need to update that URL.
Knowledge bases and AI solutions: If you index our repositories to ground a retrieval pipeline, an internal assistant, or a coding agent, update the source URLs and re-crawl. Raw file URLs move as well, so a pipeline that reads from raw.githubusercontent.com needs the GitLab raw path instead. Check this case first: a stale index does not raise an error, it quietly serves outdated content.
Git remotes: For a clone you already have, point it at the new host with git remote set-url origin https://gitlab.com/rokudev/<repo>.git.
Submodules, CI, and everything else: Update the URL in .gitmodules, then run git submodule sync. Check any pipeline that clones a repository, fetches a release artifact, or installs a package directly from a git URL. Then check bookmarks, runbooks, and internal wikis.
To find the stragglers, you can search your own repositories for rokudev and work through the hits.
Suggesting documentation fixes
You can still suggest fixes to the developer docs. Request access to the docs repository at https://gitlab.com/rokudev/dev-doc, fork it, and submit a merge request with your change. The “Suggest edits” feature is not supported on GitLab.
For more information
Roku developer repositories on GitLab: The new home for the SDK, the documentation, the samples, and the tooling repositories.
Roku developer documentation: Will be updated to point at the new repository URLs.

bbtree: fastest ordered map
B-trees are by far the most important access path structure in database and file systems.
— Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter1
1Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter, Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques (1993), as quoted by Goetz Graefe in Modern B-Tree Techniques (2011).
bbtree is by far the fastest B-tree (that I'm aware of):
5× faster than std's BTreeMap on a single thread, 12× faster than crossbeam-skiplist at 96 threads.
30% lower memory usage.
Zero dependencies, no_std compatible.
bbtree::unsync::BBTreeMap is a drop-in replacement for std's BTreeMap/BTreeSet.
Production-ready by formal verification, model checking, deterministic simulation, fuzzing, and lots of testing.

Batched: get_many_copied, 64 keys a call; insert_many, 16. scc TreeIndex and concurrent-map are concurrent maps, used from one thread. std's HashMap keeps no order, so it can't scan. It stands in for DashMap, the other cards' hash map, which is std's hash table split into shards, each behind a lock. Ryzen 9 9900X (Zen 5, 12 cores, 24 threads, 2 × 32 MiB L3, DDR5, mimalloc). Code: bbtree, scc TreeIndex, concurrent-map, crossbeam SkipMap.
On this page
What can it do?

Case 2: database index

2Minimize instructions

How do we make it correct?

Guard 2: LLMs
Guard 3: fuzzing, verification, DSTs
Reviewers of this post
What can it do?
B-trees are the most important data structure in big data systems, a fast b-tree like bbtree benefits everything on top of it: agents memory, LLM training, RAG, KV store, state caching, vector search, and more.
Here we discuss three representative use cases:
Replace skiplist in LSM-trees. In place of the skiplist of four LSM-trees, bbtree is 1.37–6.83× faster.
In-memory database index. In place of Turso's skiplists, inserts are 2.22× and indexed SELECTs 1.90× faster.
Mmap a bbtree from disk. No rebuild after a restart: the first answer comes 160–2,500× sooner than std's BTreeMap.
Case 1: faster memtable
Case 2: database index
Case 3: bbtree-mmap
All LSM-trees use an ordered map to hold recent writes in memory, the memtable. In Rust, this ordered map is usually a skiplist, like crossbeam-skiplist.
bbtree can easily replace it and is much faster. A skiplist takes a cache miss for almost every node it visits on its way down; a bbtree lookup touches a handful of cache lines (see How it works, below).
bbtree has a similar interface as crossbeam-skiplist but simpler: there is no epoch, no need to worry about when to pin or re-enter an epoch.
bbtree allows more advanced memory management:
Custom allocator is supported on day one.
It never allocates on irregular sizes (i.e., not a power of two): memory management stays easy, with no external fragmentation2
2Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, Free-Space Management, chapter 17 of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: external fragmentation is free space chopped into pieces of different sizes, so that a request can fail although the total would fit it.
.
Allocation failure can be gracefully handled.
We integrated bbtree into four LSM-trees, on each system's own benchmarks:
fjall: gets 2.47×, inserts 1.61×, write batches 3.00×.
SlateDB: gets 1.71×, puts 1.65×, write batches of 10 rows 2.36×.
Tonbo: 10M-row writes 6.83×, conflict-checked transactions 4.10×.
Lance's MemWAL index (its own skiplist): point lookups 2.19×, batched lookups 3.94×, batched puts 4.21×.
The LSM-trees of the End to End card: each system's own benchmark, one thread, Ryzen 9 9900X. The dark bar is the time per operation as shipped, the bright one inside it with bbtree; only the map changed.
Next, 2 of 3
Case 2: database index
→
How it works?
Every performance optimization should be guided by a cost model.
B-tree optimizations are simple, three easy pieces3
3Not more complicated than an operating system! Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (2016).
: we just need to remember three principles, in order:
The number of chained cache lines touched. A cache miss costs about 100 ns.
The number of instructions executed. An instruction costs about 0.5 ns.
The amount of cache coherence traffic, especially important for concurrent access. It forces a cache miss, and costs a little more than 100 ns.
1
Minimize cache misses
2
Minimize instructions
3
Minimize cache coherence traffic
With this cost model, it's clear that the most important optimization is to minimize the number of cache misses. To put it another way, for each cache miss, we want to narrow down the search space as much as we can.
Thought experiment: binary search vs linear search
Say we have a sorted array of u64s, and we want to find a target u64.
With binary search, each cache miss narrows down the search space by half.
With linear search, each cache miss narrows down the search space by cache_line_size / item_size items, which is 64 / 8 = 8.
So the break-even point is about 16 items, where binary search costs the same as linear search: two cache misses to find the target.
But there's a catch: 1. the CPU prefetcher may fetch the next cache lines on its own, which gives linear search an even bigger advantage; 2. linear search is simpler, allowing much more parallelism in the CPU pipeline. So the actual break-even point is usually higher.
64 sorted u64s, 8 to a cache line. Each step is one cache miss: binary search halves what is left, linear search rules out one line. Here binary search needs 3 misses and linear search 6; at 16 items, both need at most 2.
Pause
How does that apply to B-trees?
In a B-tree, this decides the node size4
4Jun Rao and Kenneth A. Ross, Making B+-Trees Cache Conscious in Main Memory (SIGMOD 2000).
. If we size nodes so that each holds about 16–32 items, we can always do linear search, which lets us do nice things like SIMD (in later sections).
What if the keys are Strings? Strings are different, because their bytes are stored on the heap, not inline in the node. This changes our equation completely. We no longer get 8 keys from one cache miss; instead, each key we load is its own cache miss. So we almost always want to do binary search over Strings.
A node of Strings holds each key's pointer, length and capacity; its bytes are on the heap. Every comparison of a binary search follows a pointer: 3 heap reads to find one key of 8.
Pause
How does bbtree do it? Heap keys are very common, so bbtree must handle them well. bbtree introduces inline_keys, an idea databases have used for decades5,6
5Goetz Graefe and Per-Åke Larson, B-Tree Indexes and CPU Caches (ICDE 2001).
6Goetz Graefe, More Modern B-Tree Techniques (2024): keep full keys out of the comparison stream with dense, fixed-width codes, and skip the prefix a page shares.
, similar to German strings7
7Thomas Neumann and Michael Freitag, Umbra: A Disk-Based System with In-Memory Performance (CIDR 2020); see also my post on the nature of strings.
and StringView in Arrow8
8Xiangpeng Hao and Andrew Lamb, Using StringView / German Style Strings to Make Queries Faster: Part 1, Reading Parquet and Part 2, String Operations (2024).
.
With fixed-size inline keys, we get back the benefit of one cache miss loading 8 (or more) keys. And we only load the full key when the comparison ties.
The same node with inline keys: the first 8 bytes of every key, 64 bytes, one cache line. One compare of all of them leaves a single candidate, and only it is read from the heap.
Pause
What about keys with long prefixes? Many keys, like URLs and paths, have long prefixes. If we just take the first 8 bytes as the inline key, we may compare nothing at all. bbtree addresses this with prefix_keys: the common prefix of all keys in a node9
9Rudolf Bayer and Karl Unterauer, Prefix B-Trees (TODS 1977).
. The beauty of prefix_keys is that no node has to store them. Every key in a node sorts between the two separators on either side of the node in its parent. So if those two separators share their first 20 bytes, every key in the node starts with the same 20 bytes.
Neighboring Wikipedia titles. The parent's two separators share their first 20 bytes, so every key of the child does too. Over the first 8 bytes, the keys all tie; past the shared 20, they all differ.
Pause
So each node only stores the length of its prefix, and keeps the window of each key right after it, which makes inline keys far more effective.
How does this apply to other key types, and how does it work with Rust's type system?
It's clear that String and Vec<u8> benefit from this optimization. But integers like u64 and u128 can too; we just need to mind the endianness: stored big-endian, their bytes sort in the same order as the numbers.
Four keys of one leaf of a tree of 10M random u64s, as bytes: the prefix its separators share, which the leaf skips; the 2 bytes it keeps as each inline key; and the rest, read only on a tie.
For other key types, like compound keys in structs, users can implement the InlineKey trait, and when they do, we use the inline keys wherever we can.
pub trait InlineKey: Ord {
    /// How many bytes of each inline key the nodes keep: 2, 4 or 8.
    const WIDTH: InlineWidth = InlineWidth::Eight;

    /// Bytes `offset..offset + 8` of the key's encoding, big-endian,
    /// zero past its end, which orders as the keys do.
    fn inline_key_at(&self, offset: usize) -> InlineWord;
}

// A compound key, ordered by customer, then order: its encoding is// both fields' bytes, one after the other.#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]struct OrderKey {
    customer: u32,
    order: u32,
}

impl InlineKey for OrderKey {
    fn inline_key_at(&self, offset: usize) -> InlineWord {
        let mut bytes = [0; 16];
        bytes[..4].copy_from_slice(&self.customer.to_be_bytes());
        bytes[4..8].copy_from_slice(&self.order.to_be_bytes());
        let start = offset.min(8);
        u64::from_be_bytes(bytes[start..start + 8].try_into().unwrap())
    }
}

let orders: BBTreeMap<OrderKey, u64, _> =
    BBTreeMap::with_strategy(WithInlineKey);
The trickiest part is Rust's type system. If we required every key type to implement InlineKey, bbtree couldn't be a drop-in replacement for std's BTreeMap/BTreeSet. Nightly Rust has specialization10
10RFC 1210: impl specialization, unstable since 2016 (tracking issue).
for exactly this. For stable Rust, we specialize the common types by hand: u64, i64, u128, i128, String, str, &str, Vec<u8>, &[u8], Box<str>, Box<[u8]>, [u8; 16], [u8; 20] and [u8; 32]. So without any extra work, the built-in types are optimized, and users can still implement the trait for their own types to get the full benefit.
Results
After these optimizations, we can show how many cache lines a lookup touches.
Cache lines brought in from memory per lookup that finds its key, 10M entries, one thread, Ryzen 9 9900X; lower is better.
Bonus: batch mode using Rust's async state machines
So far we have focused on maximizing the value of a cache miss: packing as much information as possible into one cache line.
There's a more advanced optimization: hiding the cost of cache misses.
The simplest way to hide latency is software prefetching: while working on one key, we prefetch the next one. This usually works well, but it isn't enough for B-trees.
This is because a B-tree's memory accesses are fundamentally chained: you don't know which node to fetch next until you have searched the current one.
But B-trees are often read or built in batches, which lets us play a trick with Rust's async state machines. A batch is one call with many keys, such as BBTreeMap's get_many_copied and insert_many: an array of keys in, an array of answers out.
The high-level idea is simple: in Rust we often treat an IO operation as a Future, and await it. In bbtree, we treat a cache miss as a Future, and await it too. Database research has interleaved lookups like this for years, by hand and with coroutines11
11Onur Kocberber, Babak Falsafi and Boris Grot, Asynchronous Memory Access Chaining (VLDB 2015); Georgios Psaropoulos et al., Interleaving with Coroutines: A Practical Approach for Robust Index Joins (VLDB 2017); Christopher Jonathan et al., Exploiting Coroutines to Attack the "Killer Nanoseconds" (VLDB 2018).
.
The code looks roughly like this (they run in a single thread):
fn get_many<const N: usize>(&self, keys: [&K; N]) -> [Option<V>; N] {
    let lanes = keys.map(|key| self.search(key));
    block_on(join_all(lanes))}
And search looks like this:
async fn search(&self, key: &K) -> Option<V> {
    let mut node = self.root();
    while node.is_internal() {
        let edge = node.search(key);
        node = node.child(edge);
        prefetch(node.header()).await;
    }
    node.get(key)}
Four u64 keys looked up together on one core, each key's search a task, from bbtree's own run of the batch; time is counted in turns. In its turn, a task reads the line it prefetched, steps down the tree, prefetches the next line and yields; while that line is on its way, the core runs the other tasks.
Pause
But we need to be very careful:
A cache miss costs 100 ns, so our Future must be as lightweight as possible. This means we can't use tokio or any general-purpose async runtime, because their overhead is already higher than a cache miss. bbtree polls its lanes with a tiny executor of its own: no allocation, no runtime.
Each async function in Rust is a state machine generated at compile time. We want this state machine to be as small as possible, so that switching between states is cheap.
There's no way to know whether a cache line is already in cache, so we have to guess. In bbtree that's not so hard: onc

title: Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month | Scientific American
content:
October 21, 2026
3 min read
Add Us On Google
Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month
For the first time, scientists can make quantum measurements on a positron particle
BY CLARA MOSKOWITZ EDITED BY LEE BILLINGS
kondensator / Shutterstock
Particle Physics
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
Sign Up for Our Free Daily Newsletter
You can’t hold antimatter in your hand or even in a regular laboratory apparatus. As soon as antimatter meets matter, the two tend to annihilate each other. This makes studying antimatter tricky. But now physicists have managed to trap a single subatomic particle of the stuff for months at a time in a way that allows them to study its quantum states.
Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way.
Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron—the antimatter counterpart of the electron.
“The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them,” says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters.
Gerald Gabrielse (top right) and his team in the lab where they trapped a positron particle for a month.Gerald Gabrielse
The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. “Every time they bang into something, there’s a chance of annihilation, but it doesn’t always happen,” Gabrielse says. “If they make it to the end, they get popped out.”
Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. “If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls,” Gabrielse says.
This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a month—and could let them do so indefinitely.
The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron’s magnetic moment—basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron’s spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state.
Recommended Stories
This weird particle may have come from a black hole exploding in another dimension
JONATHAN O'CALLAGHAN
Surprising result seen in primordial matter inside atom smasher
CLARA MOSKOWITZ
Vox’s Unexplainable and Scientific American explore the mystery of dark matter and the limits of science
RACHEL FELTMAN, JOSEPH HOWLETT, FONDA MWANGI & ALEX SUGIURA
What if we never find dark matter?
JOSEPH HOWLETT
Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. “We’re looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment,” Gabrielse says. That’s the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.
Just after the Big Bang, scientists think there were roughly equal amounts of the two. Most of the matter and antimatter must have annihilated, but a small excess of matter was somehow left over to seed the stars and planets we see. The magnetic moment measurement is just one of many realms where physicists are seeking differences between matter and antimatter to account for this profound discrepancy.
“Turn every particle to its antiparticle, look at physics through a mirror (flipping left and right) and press the ‘rewind button’ to reverse the flow of time,” says Roni Harnik, a theoretical physicist at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Batavia, Ill., who was not involved in the project. “Our most basic theories say that physics stays the same.”
If it turns out things are different—that the positron, for instance, has a different magnetic moment than the electron—then we’d have a hint about how matter won out.
“This is an exciting development,” Harnik says, “that will enable us to test a basic symmetry.”

She has been at Scientific American for more than a decade; previously she worked at Space.com. Moskowitz has reported live from rocket launches, space shuttle liftoffs and landings, suborbital spaceflight training, mountaintop observatories, and more. She has a bachelor’s degree in astronomy and physics from Wesleyan University and a graduate degree in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

title: GitHub - slee-persis/GVS5H: GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard | Fable 5 Level Coding for a Fifth the Price - or on a Single GPU · GitHub
content:
GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
GVS5H: Gorilla vs. 5 Humans
Results
Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend.
Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.
— the paper
Running the code
Needs uv and an API key for the model you want to test.

MULTIAGENT_MODEL=openai:gpt-5.6-terra \
uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with 'datasets<4' --with numpy --with anthropic \
  python escalation/run_bench.py --engine multiagent --only lcb --lcb 100 --parallel 8
--engine multiagent runs the manager; --engine single is the one-call baseline.
Other models: anthropic:<model>, dashscope:<model>, openrouter:<model>, each with its own *_API_KEY.
The pass@1 score prints at the end. Results are written to runs/results.json, workspaces to runs/ws/.

title: How close can pure FP get to C?
content:
How close can pure FP get to C?
October 22, 2026
In Why Lean is Faster Than Rust, the author shares an impressive result: a DEFLATE compression library written in Lean 4, a functional programming language and proof assistant, outperforming an equivalent Rust package that crates.io says has been downloaded over a billion times. From the article:
lean-zip beats every single compression level miniz_oxide provides, i.e. we're capable of providing the same compression at higher throughput. At its fastest setting we're 15% quicker and the output is 8.8% smaller.
However, the article also notes that while they managed to surpass Rust's miniz_oxide, they were no match for the end boss of DEFLATE performance: libdeflate, written in C.
lean-zip is certainly not the best here: libdeflate unsurprisingly blows it out of the water (unsurprisingly because this is a very carefully tuned implementation using architecture-specific SIMD, that we can't touch in Lean).
Enter Roc, a functional programming language (but not a theorem prover) with an explicit focus on runtime performance.
Roc's tagline is "Fast, Friendly, Functional," and Fast comes first because both running fast and compiling fast have always been central goals. Roc is not a mature language (it's still weeks away from its first numbered release, 0.1.0), and its nascent package ecosystem has had almost no optimization work done on it. Still, between its language design, longstanding optimizations, and brand-new compiler implementation, I figured Roc already had enough of a foundation in place to take on the champ: libdeflate.
So I spent a bunch of time grinding through performance optimizations on roc-deflate, a package Niclas Ahden wrote (and uses in paid production work) for DEFLATE compression. I didn't expect to beat libdeflate's performance across the board, but I wanted to see how close it could get on the non-streaming APIs (as roc-deflate hasn't implemented streaming yet), using the classic Silesia corpus for benchmarking and verifying that it produced identical outputs.
Under 10% Slower
Here's where the benchmarks stand today, running on the 2021 M1 MacBook Pro where I did all the optimization work, as well as on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X Ubuntu machine for an x64 comparison.
roc-deflate ran these 144 benchmarks slower on average than libdeflate, in the median case 8.9% slower on the Ryzen 3900X, and 2.6% on the M1 MacBook Pro.

So while we didn't outperform the champ on average, a median slowdown percentage in the single digits compared to such a carefully-tuned SIMD-powered C library is wild. It's frankly not a result I knew was achievable going in, since Roc is a functional language with automatic memory management racing against code that doesn't have to do bounds checks. (Bounds checks have a cost, but then again, the last time a skipped bounds check in C compression code led to a major Remote Code Execution vulnerability was yesterday.)
The graph shows more detail than just the median gap. On the worst-case inputs, roc-deflate was 18% slower than libdeflate, but on the best-case inputs, roc-deflate was slightly over 18% faster! That's not because Roc has some magical optimization that C can't access; it's just that the two implementations are different, and although on average roc-deflate is slower, for certain inputs it happens to be faster. So while it's possible to get a speedup by switching from libdeflate to roc-deflate, you shouldn't expect it on average.
To be clear, C's performance ceiling is higher than Roc's. For any input where roc-deflate currently outperforms libdeflate, C code can close that gap. The reverse is not true; Roc code is memory-safe, does automatic reference counting, checks bounds, and supports no Rust-style unsafe to opt out of any of that. These properties give Roc code stronger safety guarantees than code written in C, Zig, Rust, and other languages that allow full access to the hardware—and the price it pays for those guarantees is a lower performance ceiling.
Obviously we can't extrapolate from this one result about how close Roc can get to C in the general case, but now something has been demonstrated that nobody knew was achievable before. As far as I know, this is the most optimization effort that has been put into any Roc package to date, so how close others can get to this result is a complete unknown right now. So while I'm thrilled by this result, I'm fully aware that we won't know how well it generalizes until we've optimized a wider sample of real-world Roc code bases!
What the Performance Gap Buys
An obvious question is "Why settle for any amount slower?" If you could get C levels of performance, why not use libdeflate itself and close that remaining gap?
A pure-Roc implementation has several advantages over a pure-C one:
Memory safety. Roc code is fully memory-safe and has no language primitives that let you opt out of it. This code is only able to approach C levels of performance because Roc's optimization pipeline determined that many bounds checks and reference counting operations were provably safe to optimize away. Compression packages written in pure Roc don't have access to the unchecked memory operation that caused yesterday's Brotli Remote Code Execution vulnerability.
No side effects. Roc's type system infers which functions are pure and which can perform side effects. Pure functions' types use a thin arrow, like Bool -> Bool, whereas effectful functions use a thick arrow, like Bool => Bool. (As with memory safety, Roc enforces this and supports no way to opt out.) So when you see that roc-deflate's functions have only thin arrows in their annotations, you know they really are pure functions.
Supply-Chain Security. Roc does not have an arbitrary FFI, meaning you know for sure that roc-deflate's pure functions can't even attempt to do I/O or access arbitrary memory. Given the explosion in supply chain attacks, it's valuable to know that the damage a malicious actor can do with a pure function in a compromised Roc package is limited to returning the wrong value, crashing, or wasting system resources. Roc packages also don't support build scripts, which was the vector used to successfully compromise the popular Rust arrayref package two months ago.
Portability. Roc pure functions are designed to be extremely deterministic: they always return the same values when given the same arguments—not just when run on the same machine, but also on any target you compile that code to. (The functions may also crash or fail to terminate, but that behavior should also be deterministic across targets.) The only way a Roc pure function should be expected to behave differently when run on two different systems is if one system runs out of memory mid-execution.
If any of these guarantees don't hold in practice, it can only be due to a defect in Roc's compiler, the platform the application is running on, or the underlying hardware. So when you see in roc-deflate's docs that the entire package is 100% pure functions, you can be confident you are getting all of the above properties from everything the package has to offer. The type system enforces it!
The reason we've been working so hard on all this might become clearer if you look at the proposition in reverse: would you give up guaranteed memory safety, guaranteed lack of side effects, guaranteed deterministic behavior across all targets, and the security benefits of having no exploitable build scripts in packages...for an average speedup percentage in the single digits?
That answer can legitimately vary by use case—Roc's own compiler, for example, wants the maximum performance the hardware can deliver—but I bet a lot of people reading this can see why we're so excited to have achieved this result.
Roc-Specific Optimizations
Most of the optimizations that improved roc-deflate's numbers came from general optimization techniques that are widely beneficial across languages. (I always recommend Casey Muratori's Performance-Aware Programming Series, which I paid for and learned a lot from.) Some of the optimization techniques were Roc-specific, though, and I wanted to mention them here as a reference for others. Even if you're not writing Roc code, this can also give you an idea of how Roc achieves its performance.
Avoid Unnecessary Sharing
One of Roc's most effective optimizations is opportunistic mutation (which Koka calls "Functional but In-Place"). You can learn how it works in Roc's docs on opportunistic mutation, but from a performance optimization perspective, it's critically important to avoid unnecessary sharing so that values remain unique and therefore eligible for in-place mutation.
Hoist Bounds Checks
You can't opt out of bounds checks (e.g. getting a value out of a dynamically-sized collection) in Roc like you can in C, Zig, and Rust, but Roc's compiler can optimize them away if it knows they'd be guaranteed to pass. Bounds checks are most costly inside loops, so you can get a lot of mileage out of adding something like if collection.len() <= highest_index_used { return 0 } before the loop starts. This adds an additional check that looks redundant, but it can allow the optimizer to safely delete costlier checks inside the loop, once it can tell that failures would not be reachable after that early return.
Build Lookup Tables at Compile Time
Roc's compile-time evaluation can be used to assemble lookup tables at compile time as long as nothing depends on runtime inputs. Even better, since their lengths are known at compile time, you can do things like Ok(entry) = lookup_table.get(5) to do an exhaustive pattern match that Roc's compiler will know is valid thanks to compile-time evaluation. This avoids runtime bounds checks that non-constant tables might have to pay for.
Consider Wrapping Arithmetic
In Roc, a + b desugars to a.plus(b). For an integer like U64, U64.plus includes an overflow check, whereas plus_wrap does not. Although plus is the safer default, overflow checks have a runtime cost, as CPUs can do wrapping integer arithmetic in one instruction. When Roc's compiler can prove that overflow won't occur, both plus and plus_wrap will optimize to the same instructions, but when it can't, you may get a speedup by choosing plus_wrap.
Room for Improvement
I'm sure there are still opportunities to improve roc-deflate's performance—especially on x64 CPUs—as well as the optimization pipeline in Roc's compiler.
At this point I feel reasonably confident that all the low-hanging fruit has been picked, but if anyone wants to try it out for themselves, here's the script I ran to set up and run the benchmark suite on Linux. (Note that Claude Opus 5.5 generated this script, and I haven't vetted it for security; run it outside a sandbox at your own risk!) It pins both Roc compiler revisions and roc-deflate versions, so you'll want to adjust those commits if you're trying out potential improvements.
For my part, I'll be focusing on the upcoming Roc 0.1.0 release from now until it's out. It's been eight years in the making, so I'll be very happy for us to finally have a numbered release! If you'd like to learn more about Roc, check out roc-lang.org or come say hi on Roc Zulip!

title: AI Image Generation | danielball.com
content:
AI Image Generation
This is my general guide to AI image generation. It covers how the models work at a high level, the different types, a bit of history, what you actually get from ChatGPT and how to build image generation into your own code and agents.
It’s based on my own experiments calling a handful of image providers from Python. I’ve generated pixel art sprites, photorealistic card table backgrounds and a series of restaurant posters, trying to make one that doesn’t look AI generated. Every image here came from those experiments.
TLDR
A short history

How it works

Are multimodal models diffusion under the hood?
How they compare

Ways to use it

What it costs

Prompting that works

Marketing is where AI images get the most criticism
Making a poster that doesn’t look AI generated
Prompting rules of thumb
Pixel art
Pixel art is a style, not a format
Many sprites on one canvas
Doing pixel art properly
Where the line falls
Integrating image generation into a coding project
Put a thin interface in front of every provider
Expect the ground to move

Do the exact work in code
Test without spending money
Integrating with an agent

Tips for agent-driven generation
Glossary
Resources
TLDR
Most models start from noise and clean it up. Text steers the clean-up. Newer models also plan the image the way a chat model plans a sentence.
You pay for the canvas, not the content. A plain wooden table costs the same as a detailed oil painting of the same size.
ChatGPT is the easiest way in and the hardest to control. Great for one-off images and conversational edits. For anything repeatable you want the API.
Prices vary more than 100 times over. Anything from a fraction of a cent to 15 cents or more per image. Running a model locally costs nothing. The cheapest model isn’t always the cheapest result.
The APIs move under you. Models get retired with weeks of notice and providers quietly ignore parameters. Keep the model in config and log what you actually got back.
Describe how it was made, not how it should look. Camera, film, print process and layout get better results than “stunning” and “hyper-detailed”.
Spelling and fingers are no longer the giveaway. The tell now is taste. Too much glow, too much drama and nothing allowed to be plain.
Agents are good at this. A multimodal agent can write the prompt, call the API, look at the result and try again. You still need to supply the taste.
The best pipelines are hybrids. Let AI do the creative part. Let ordinary code do the exact parts like sizing, transparency, palettes and layout.
A short history
2014 - GANs. Ian Goodfellow’s generative adversarial networks pit two networks against each other, one making images and one spotting fakes. They go on to produce convincing synthetic faces but are hard to steer with text.
2015 - DeepDream. Google’s Inceptionism experiments turn image recognition inside out. The results are full of psychedelic dog faces, because the network was trained on a dataset with a lot of dogs in it.
2018 - AI art goes to auction. A blurry GAN portrait called Edmond de Belamy sells at Christie’s for $432,500, more than 40 times its top estimate.
2019 - Faces that don’t exist. NVIDIA’s StyleGAN powers thispersondoesnotexist.com, a new photorealistic fake face on every refresh.
2021 - DALL-E. OpenAI links text and images in one model. You can type a sentence and get a picture, even if it’s a small, blurry one.
2022 - The breakout year. DALL-E 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion all arrive within a few months. Stable Diffusion is open source and runs on a gaming PC with about 7GB of video memory, which kicks off a huge community of fine-tunes and tools.
2023 - Photorealism and readable text. A Midjourney image of the Pope in a white puffer jacket fools much of the internet. Ideogram launches with text you can actually read. SDXL raises the bar for open models and DALL-E 3 moves into ChatGPT.
2024 - Flux and the backlash. Former Stable Diffusion researchers found Black Forest Labs and release Flux, which becomes the default open-weight model. Meanwhile AI posters become a byword for cutting corners (more on that below).
2025 - Native image models. OpenAI builds image generation into GPT-4o itself and the “Studio Ghibli” trend takes over social media. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, nicknamed Nano Banana, makes conversational editing cheap at $0.039 an image.
2026 - Abundance and churn. OpenAI switches off DALL-E in its API. OpenRouter alone lists over 60 image models from a dozen companies, and older models are retired every few months.
Six fingers and gibberish text
For a few years the easiest way to spot an AI image was to count the fingers or try to read the sign in the background. Both problems are now mostly fixed, and why they happened says a lot about how these models work.
Hands are complicated, flexible and usually partly hidden in photos. Behind a cup, in a pocket, half out of frame. The models learned what hands look like as a texture, not how many fingers they have. Midjourney v5 in March 2023 was widely reported as the turning point. Experts suspected better curated training data with clearer pictures of hands, plus bigger models and higher resolutions. It wasn’t perfect. People in the background still had alien anatomy for a while.
Text had a more specific cause. Most models read your prompt through a tokeniser that splits it into chunks of words rather than letters. The model never sees that “chocolate” is spelled c-h-o-c-o-l-a-t-e, so it can’t draw it letter by letter. A 2022 paper, Character-Aware Models Improve Visual Text Rendering, showed that giving the model access to individual characters fixed much of the problem. Ideogram, whose team included former Google Imagen researchers, made text a selling point in 2023. By 2025 the multimodal models from OpenAI and Google, which understand language as well as any chatbot, had made readable text normal.
The fix arrived in stages, and the old problem leaked into the real world in between. The Willy’s Chocolate Experience in Glasgow in February 2024 promised “a pasadise of sweet teats” on its AI-generated posters. Long text is still not completely solved. In December 2025 Nano Banana Pro turned “Lived experience” into Liver experience on an otherwise good infographic.
How it works
You don’t need the maths to use these models well. You do need a rough picture of what’s going on, because it explains most of the surprises.
Diffusion models
Most image models are diffusion models. During training they learn to remove noise from images. Take a photo, add a bit of static and teach the model to predict what the clean version looked like. Repeat billions of times at every level of noise.
To generate, you run that in reverse. Start from pure static and remove a little noise at a time over a number of steps. A text encoder turns your prompt into numbers that steer each step towards an image that matches it.
Two details matter in practice.
They work in a compressed space. Latent diffusion, the approach behind Stable Diffusion, paints on an internal canvas about 8 times smaller on each side than the final image, then decodes it. That’s why you can’t ask for a 32 x 32 image. The internal canvas would be 4 x 4.
Steps cost time. More steps is slower and usually better, up to a point. “Distilled” models like Flux Schnell and SDXL Turbo are trained to get a good image in 4 steps instead of 30.
Multimodal models
The newer approach puts image generation inside a model that also understands language. Because the same model reads your prompt and makes the picture, these are much better at following instructions, rendering text and editing an image you give them. GPT Image, Gemini’s image models and Meta’s Muse work this way. Some reason about the layout before they draw, which makes a real difference when the prompt is about where things go.
Are multimodal models diffusion under the hood?
Often partly, and the line is blurrier than the marketing suggests.
OpenAI’s launch post for GPT-4o image generation hints at a hybrid. A language model plans the image as a sequence of tokens, the same way it writes a sentence, and a diffusion-style decoder paints the final pixels. Google hasn’t published how its Gemini image models work. Going the other way, modern “diffusion” models like Flux use transformer blocks that process text and image together, which is the same building block as a chat model.
So the useful distinction isn’t the maths. It’s how deeply the image model understands language. That’s what gives you instruction following, readable text and editing.
How they compare
  Diffusion models (Flux, SDXL, Imagen) Multimodal models (GPT Image, Gemini, Muse)
What drives cost Resolution and number of steps Image tokens, usually fixed per size and quality tier
Strengths Cheap, fast, runs locally, seeds give repeatable results Follows instructions, renders text, edits from a reference image
Weaknesses Takes prompts more literally Often no seed control and a fixed output size
Open weights? Often Rarely
Seeds
The random static a diffusion model starts from is set by a seed. Same seed, same prompt and same model gives the same image. That’s what makes batches repeatable. Many hosted models ignore or reject seeds, so don’t build anything that depends on them without checking.
Types of image generation
“Image generation” covers several different jobs. Most providers support some of them, not all.
Type What it does Example use Where to try it
Text to image A prompt becomes a picture Concept art, backgrounds, placeholders OpenAI image guide
Image editing “Make the mug blue” on an existing image Iterating on a design without starting again Gemini image docs
Reference images Keep a character, product or style consistent The same knight in eight poses Gemini image docs
Inpainting Regenerate one masked area Removing an object, fixing a hand Diffusers inpainting guide
Outpainting Extend an image past its edges Turning a square into a banner ComfyUI inpaint and outpaint examples
Structural control Follow a sketch, pose or depth map Matching a layout exactly ControlNet and the Diffusers ControlNet guide
Fine-tuning (LoRA) Teach an open model a new style or subject A consistent house style or product Diffusers LoRA training
Upscaling Add detail at a higher resolution Finishing the keepers from a cheap batch Real-ESRGAN
Background removal Cut the subject out Transparent sprites and product shots rembg
Text to vector Produce SVG instead of pixels Icons and logos Recraft
Tileable textures are worth a special mention. Plain models won’t reliably produce a seamless tile. You need a model or LoRA trained for it or a tiling option in the tool.
Ways to use it
Route Examples Good for Watch out for
Chat apps ChatGPT, Gemini One-off images, quick edits Little control, usage limits
Creative tools Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, Canva Designers, polished results Subscriptions, hard to automate
Direct APIs OpenAI, Google Gemini and Vertex AI Production code Each API is different
Aggregators OpenRouter, Replicate, fal.ai Trying many models with one key Markup on some, models come and go
Local Flux or SDXL with mflux or ComfyUI Free bulk generation, full control Needs a decent GPU or Apple Silicon, slower
For my experiments I deliberately avoided subscriptions. Everything was pay per image through an API or was run locally.
What you get with ChatGPT
Most people’s first experience of AI images is typing a request into ChatGPT. It’s worth knowing what you’re getting.
ChatGPT uses OpenAI’s own GPT Image models, which have been built into the chat since March 2025.
Is DALL-E still a thing? Not really. DALL-E 3 was ChatGPT’s image generator from October 2023 until the switch to GPT-4o image generation in March 2025. OpenAI then removed DALL-E 2 and 3 from its API on 12 May 2026. The name lives on mostly as a generic term for AI images.
What it’s good at
Conversation. You can say “warmer light” or “move the mug to the left” and it edits rather than starting again.
Following instructions. It handles layouts, counts and specific details better than older diffusion models.
Text. Signs, posters and labels are usually spelled correctly.
References. Upload a photo or sketch and it will work from it.
What it’s not good at
Control. You get a handful of aspect ratios, no seed and no way to run a batch. You can’t ask for exactly 1024 x 512.
Speed. Each image takes anything from a few seconds to over a minute, and there are usage limits, especially on the free plan.
A house style. Left to itself it drifts towards a recognisable look. The 2025 model was known for a warm yellow cast nicknamed the “piss filter”. Describe the lighting and colour you want rather than leaving it to the defaults.
Content rules. It will refuse some requests, like real public figures in certain contexts or close copies of copyrighted characters.
Provenance. OpenAI adds both C2PA metadata and a SynthID watermark to its images, according to its help centre. Google adds SynthID to Gemini images. Metadata is easily stripped. Watermarks survive screenshots better, but neither is something to rely on if you’re trying to prove an image is or isn’t AI.
ChatGPT or the API? The same family of models is available through OpenAI’s API, billed per image. The API gives you sizes from a fixed list, quality tiers, batching from code and, on some models, transparent backgrounds. If you need more than a few images or the same kind of image repeatedly, use the API. The Gemini app versus the Gemini API is the same story.
What it costs
You pay for the canvas
The most useful mental model I’ve found is a painter who only owns large canvases, charges per canvas and paints every square inch with the same care. A flat blue sky gets as much effort as a face.
Simple pictures aren’t cheaper. The model does the same work across the whole image.
You can’t generate small. Models work best at roughly 512 to 1600 pixels. For a 32 x 32 sprite you generate a big picture and shrink it yourself.
Asking for a smaller size often doesn’t help. Gemini 2.5 Flash Image returned 1024 x 1024 when I asked for 512 x 512, at the same flat price.
Four ways you get billed
Billing model Examples Does making it smaller help?
Flat per image Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, Recraft No
Per image, tiered by size and quality Newer Gemini models, OpenAI GPT Image A little. The smallest tier is still a big canvas for most needs
Per megapixel or GPU-second Replicate, fal.ai, most models on OpenRouter Yes
Your own electricity Local Flux Yes, and speed is what you save
The landscape i

THE NETWORK
Emergency Action Messages are the coded traffic of the US nuclear forces, read aloud in the phonetic alphabet on the High Frequency Global Communications System. The primary frequency is 11175 kHz, upper sideband, and anyone with a shortwave radio can hear it.
Why shortwave? HF bounces off the ionosphere, so one transmitter reaches thousands of miles with nothing in between. Its weakness is the same sky: a nuclear burst floods the ionosphere with electrons and HF gets absorbed instead of reflected. So HFGCS is one path among several. It's the one you can hear, and because every message is encrypted, hearing it is all anyone outside the force can do.

THE CAPSULE
The messages you can hear above are meant for rooms like this one. The capsule is where an EAM lands: a command post passes it down, the console takes it in, and the crew acts on it. If an order to launch ever came, this is how it would arrive.
Sixty feet down, behind an eight-ton blast door, two officers sit a 24-hour alert in a room the size of a school bus.
The crew commander sits left, the deputy right. Between them: the launch control console, the printers, the phones, and the shelf of procedures that governs every minute.
A missile combat crew on alert. The red clock above the binders keeps Zulu time — the time every message to the capsule is written in. The crew checks it every day against the U.S. Naval Observatory's master clock, to the second.

BINDER 4
THE CREW
A missile combat crew is two officers, a commander and a deputy. They go to the field together, take the capsule over from the crew before them, and hold it for 24 hours.
The day has a shape.
When a message comes in, both officers have to agree it is authentic before anything else happens.
A flight commander, left, and a deputy flight commander of the 10th Missile Squadron check their communications equipment at a launch control center near Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana, 16 March 2015.
U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Dillon Johnston, 341st Missile Wing Public Affairs. VIRIN 150316-F-HA826-128. Public domain.
A missile combat crew commander, 319th Missile Squadron, and her deputy commander simulate key turns of the Minuteman III weapon system in the E-01 Launch Control Center, F.E. Warren Air Force Base missile complex, Wyoming, 9 February 2016.
U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Jason Wiese, 90th Missile Wing. VIRIN 160209-F-BR137-127. Public domain.
FROM THE MESSAGE TO THE KEYS
1THE MESSAGE
An order reaches the capsule as an emergency action message, an EAM. A command post passes the coded message to the launch control centers under it. In the capsule the message comes in through the console's communications element, which handles messages from higher authority and processes emergency action messages. It is the same kind of message you can copy above.
Sources: HD 2001 p. 7 · HD 2001 p. 3 · REACT fact sheet
2AUTHENTICATE
Before acting, the crew has to authenticate the message. Only when both officers agree the message is authentic do they go on.
Sources: NPS HRS p. 115 · HD 2001 p. 7
3TWO OFFICERS, TWO KEYS
The system was built so that no single person could launch a missile. A crew is two officers, a commander and a deputy, and each has a launch key. In the Cold War capsule preserved at Delta-01, the two key switches were 12 feet apart. The console is the REACT system, fitted in 1995 and 1996. In the 2016 photograph above, the two officers sit side by side at the console, each at their own panel; the Air Force caption says they are simulating key turns. The launch switches are on separate panels of that console, and the keys are still turned together.
Sources: NPS HRS p. 85 · HAER CO-84 p. 10 · NMUSAF "Missile Combat Crews" · SAC guide p. 7 · NPS TwHP, Reading 3 · HD 2001 pp. 20, 24 · DVIDS 2406843 · DVIDS 2991929 · HD 2001 p. 7
4TWO CAPSULES
One crew's keys are not enough, because the system was also built so that no single crew could launch. Normally a second capsule has to vote as well. Without that corroborating signal from another launch control center, the missile does not launch.
Sources: NPS HRS p. 85 · HD 2001 p. 7 · DVIDS 2406843 · DVIDS 2991929 · NPS HRS p. 115
5WHAT A CAPSULE REACHES
Each capsule has primary control of the ten missiles in its flight. Five flights make a squadron of 50, and each of its five capsules can command and monitor all 50. Today the force is 400 Minuteman III missiles in three wings: F.E. Warren in Wyoming, Malmstrom in Montana and Minot in North Dakota.
Sources: HD 2001 p. 7 · NPS HRS p. 28 · AF LGM-30G fact sheet, current as of February 2019
6HOW MANY?
That's in the order. Nobody outside the force knows, and we don't guess.
